(p-154) Sūrat Yūsuf is Meccan, and its verses number one hundred and eleven.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Clear Book.﴾ "These" (tilka) is a demonstrative referring to the verses of the sūrah, and it is these that are meant by "the Book." That is, these verses are the verses of the sūrah, whose matter is manifest in its inimitability (i'jaz), or whose meanings are clear, or which make clear to whoever reflects upon them that it is from Allah. Or it refers to what the Jews asked, for it is related that their scholars told the leaders of the polytheists: "Ask Muhammad why the family of Ya'qub moved from Syria to Egypt, and about the story of Yusuf (peace be upon him)." Then the following was revealed: ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down﴾, i.e., the Book. ﴿As an Arabic Qur'an﴾. He called a part of it "Qur'an," because in origin it is a generic noun (ism jins) that applies to the whole and the part, and it has become a proper name for the whole by predominance (ghalaba). Its being in the accusative is as a circumstantial qualifier (hal). As for the word itself, it is either a preparatory qualifier (tawti'ah) for the circumstantial qualifier which is ﴿Arabic﴾, or it is a circumstantial qualifier because it is a verbal noun (masdar) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul). ﴿Arabic﴾ is either an attribute of it, or a circumstantial qualifier from the pronoun within it, or a circumstantial qualifier following another circumstantial qualifier; and on all of this there is difference of opinion. ﴿So that you may understand﴾ is the cause (illah) of its being sent down with this attribute, i.e., We sent it down gathered together or recited in your language, so that you may comprehend it and grasp its meanings; or that you may employ your intellects in it, so that you may know that its narrating the story in this manner from one who did not learn stories is a miracle that can only be conceived through revelation (wahy).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 3:

﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾ (aḥsan al-qaṣaṣ), the best of narration (aḥsan al-iqtiṣāṣ), because it is narrated in the most wondrous of styles; or [it is the best of stories] because of what it includes of wonders, wisdom, signs and lessons. Here qaṣaṣ is on the pattern of faʿal in the sense of mafʿūl (object), like naqḍ (what is broken) and salb (what is plundered). Its derivation is from qaṣṣa atharahu, meaning he followed his trace. ﴿By what We have revealed to you﴾, i.e., by Our revelation. ﴿This Qur'an﴾, meaning the surah. It is also permissible to make this (hādhā) the object of naqussu ʿalayka, with aḥsan being in the accusative as an infinitive (maṣdar). ﴿And indeed you were before it among the heedless﴾, i.e., regarding this story; it had never occurred to you nor had it ever struck your hearing. This is a justification for its being revealed. The particle in (wa-in) is the lightened form of the heavy (inna), and the lām is the lām that distinguishes it (al-lām al-fāriqa).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 4:

﴿When Yusuf said﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "the best of stories" if the latter is taken as the object (maf'ul) in a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal); or it is in the accusative by an implied "remember" (udhkur). ﴿Yusuf﴾ is Hebrew; had it been Arabic, it would have been declined (lu surifa). It is also read with a fatha and a kasra on the sin (as-sin), meaning "to be toyed with" (al-tala'ub bihi), not as an imperfect verb in the passive or active voice from "asafa" (to grieve), because the well-known reading attests to its being non-Arabic (ajamah).

﴿to his father﴾ Ya'qub ibn Is'haq ibn Ibrahim, peace be upon them all. And from him, peace and blessings be upon him, [the Prophet said]: "The noble, son of the noble, son of the noble, son of the noble: Yusuf ibn Ya'qub ibn Is'haq ibn Ibrahim."

﴿O my father﴾: its original form is "ya abi", and the ta' of feminine (ta' al-ta'nith) was substituted for the ya' (of the first person), so that the two correspond in being an addition. For this reason Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub changed it to a ha' when stopping (fi al-waqf), and they kasra-d it because it is a substitute for a letter that corresponds to it. Ibn 'Amir read it with a fatha throughout the Qur'an (p-155) because it is the vowel of its original form, or because the original was "ya abata", so the alif was dropped and the fatha remained. "Ya abata" is permissible, but "ya abati" is not, because it combines the substitute and what is substituted. It is also read with a damma, treating it like feminine nouns ending in ta' without considering the substitution. It was not made sukun as its original form was, because it is a sound letter placed in the position of a noun, so it must be vowelled, like the kaf of address (kaf al-khitab).

﴿Indeed I saw﴾: from ru'ya (dream), not from ru'yah (sight), because of His saying: ﴿Do not recount your dream﴾ and His saying: ﴿This is the interpretation of my dream from before﴾.

﴿eleven stars, and the sun and the moon﴾. It is narrated from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, that "a Jew came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'Tell me, O Muhammad, about the stars that Yusuf saw.' He remained silent, then Jibril (peace be upon him) descended and informed him of that. He said: 'If I inform you, will you become Muslim?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Jaryan, al-Tariq, al-Dhayyal, Qabis, Amudan, al-Fulayq, al-Mushbih, al-Darrih, al-Furugh, Wathab, and Dhu al-Kaftayn; Yusuf saw them, and the sun and the moon descended from the sky and prostrated to him.' The Jew said: 'Yes, by Allah, these are their names.'"

﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾: this is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining their state in which he saw them, so there is no repetition. They were treated as rational beings (majra al-'uqala') because they are described with their attributes.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 5:**

﴿He said, "O my son"﴾: *Bunayy* is the diminutive of *ibn* (son). He used the diminutive either out of affection or because of his young age, for he was twelve years old. Hafs (one of the transmitters of the Qur'an) read *yā bunayya* here and in "al-Ṣāffāt" with a *fatḥa* on the *yā'* (the final vowel of the diminutive).

﴿Do not relate your dream to your brothers, lest they plot against you a scheme﴾: *Fa-yakīdū* means they will devise a stratagem to destroy you. Ya'qub (peace be upon him) understood from his dream that God would choose him for His message and make him superior to his brothers, so he feared their envy and their hostility. *Al-ru'yā* (the dream) is like *al-ru'ya* (the sight), except that it is specific to what occurs in sleep. The two are distinguished by the feminine suffixes, as with *al-qurba* (nearness, in the sense of an act of devotion) and *al-qurbā* (kinship). The dream is the impression of an image that descends from the horizon of the *mutakhayyila* (the imaginative faculty) onto the *ḥiss al-mushtarak* (the common sense, the faculty that unifies the data of the five senses). A true dream arises only when the soul connects with the *malakūt* (the unseen realm of the heavens) because of the affinity between them, at the moment when the soul is freed, even slightly, from managing the body. The soul then perceives, through what it contains, the meanings that are appropriate to it and that are present there. Then the imaginative faculty represents these meanings in a form that suits them and sends it to the common sense, where it becomes something seen. If that form is very closely related to the meaning, such that the difference is only one of generality and particularity, the dream needs no interpretation. Otherwise it requires interpretation.

*Kāda* (to be about to) is followed by *li-* (the preposition *lām*), although it is transitive by itself, because it contains the sense of *faʿala* (to do), which takes that preposition. This is for emphasis. For the same reason it is reinforced with the verbal noun (*kayd*), and its cause is given in His words:

﴿Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy﴾: he is evidently hostile, because of what he did to Adam (peace be upon him) and Hawwa (Eve). He spares no effort in adorning [sins] for them and stirring up envy among them, until it drives them to scheming.

And thus (ﷺ)... wait, let me translate precisely.

**"And thus"** — that is: just as He chose you for such a dream, which indicates nobility, honour and perfection of soul. **"Your Lord will choose you"** — for prophethood and dominion, or for great affairs. Al-ijtiba' (choosing) is derived from *jabayta al-shay'*, when you gather a thing for yourself. **"And He will teach you"** — this is a new sentence, separate from the simile, as if it were said: "and He teaches you." **"Of the interpretation of events"** — of the interpretation of dreams, since they are "events" (ahadith): from the King if they are true, and from the self or Satan if they are false. Or, of the interpretation of the obscure parts of the books of God the Exalted, the practices (sunan) of the prophets, and the words of the wise. Al-ahadith is a collective noun (ism jam') for hadith, just as abatil is a collective noun for batil (falsehood). **"And He will complete His favour upon you"** — by prophethood, or by joining the blessing of this world to the blessing of the Hereafter. **"And upon the family of Ya'qub"** — he means all his sons. Perhaps he inferred their prophethood from the light of the stars, or from their offspring. **"Just as He completed it upon your two fathers"** — with the message. It has been said: upon Ibrahim with friendship (khullah) and deliverance from the fire, and upon Ishaq by rescuing him from the slaughter and ransoming him with a great sacrifice. **"Before"** — that is, before you, or before this time. **"Ibrahim and Ishaq"** — an explanatory apposition (atf bayan) to "your two fathers." **"Indeed your Lord is All-Knowing"** — of who deserves to be chosen. **"All-Wise"** — He does things in the manner that is fitting.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 7:

﴿Indeed, in Joseph and his brothers﴾, i.e., in their story, ﴿are signs﴾, indications of the power and wisdom of Allah the Exalted, or signs of your prophethood. Ibn Kathir recited it as «āyatun» (singular). ﴿For those who ask﴾, for whoever inquires about their story. By "his brothers" is meant the ten half-brothers (banū ʿillāt), and they are: Yahudha (Judah), Ruwbil (Reuben), Shamʿun (Simeon), Lawi (Levi), Zabalun (Zebulun), Yashkhar (Issachar), and Dinah from the daughter of his maternal aunt Layya, whom Yaʿqub (Jacob) first married. When she died, he married her sister Rahil (Rachel), and she bore him Binyamin (Benjamin) and Yusuf (Joseph). It is said that he combined the two sisters, and combining them was not forbidden at that time, and [there were] four others: Dan, Naftali (Naphtali), Jad (Gad), and Asher, from two concubines, Zulfa and Balha.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 8:

﴿When they said: Joseph and his brother [Benjamin] are dearer to our father than we are,﴾ [Benjamin is named explicitly, and his being singled out by the phrase "his brother" is because he was a brother to Joseph from both parents (lit. "from both sides").] ﴿though we are a group (ʿuṣbah)﴾ [meaning: while the situation is that we are a group of strong men, more deserving of affection than two young boys who are of no use, since neither of them can provide support]. The ʿuṣbah (group) and the iṣābah (band) are ten or more; they were so named because affairs are bound together (taʿṣabu) by them. ﴿Our father is surely in clear error﴾ [for preferring the lesser over the greater, or for failing to be even-handed in affection].

It is narrated that he loved him more because of the signs of excellence he saw in him, and his brothers were envious of him. When he saw the dream, his love for him doubled to the point that he could not bear to be apart from him, so their envy intensified until it drove them to target him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 12, verses 9–10:

﴿Kill Joseph﴾ is part of what is related after His saying, "when they said." It seems they had agreed upon that matter, except for the one who said, ﴿Do not kill Joseph.﴾ It is said that this was said only by Shim'un or Dan, and the others consented to it.

﴿Or cast him into some land﴾ unknown and far from inhabited areas. This is the meaning of its being indefinite and unspecified, and for this reason it is put in the accusative like the adverbials of unspecified place (*zuruf mubhama*). ﴿Your father's face will be free for you﴾ is the answer to the command (*jawab al-amr*). The meaning is: your father's face will be turned toward you, he will face you entirely, will not look away from you toward anyone else, and no one will compete with you in his love. ﴿And you will be﴾ is put in the jussive by coordination with *yakhlu*, or put in the accusative by an implied *an*. ﴿After him﴾ means after Joseph, or after finishing with his affair, or after his killing or casting away. ﴿A righteous people﴾ means repentant to God Most High for what you have committed, or righteous with your father by reconciling between you and him with an excuse you prepare, or righteous in your worldly affairs, for these will be arranged for you after that, with the clearing of your father's face.

﴿One speaker among them said﴾ meaning Yahudha, who was the best of them in his opinion regarding him. It is said it was Ruwbil. ﴿Do not kill Joseph,﴾ for killing is a grave matter. ﴿And throw him into the bottom of the well﴾ into its depths. It was named *ghayabat* because of his being hidden from the eyes of onlookers. Nafi' read *ghayabat* in both places in the plural, as if that well had many depths. It was also read *ghaybat* and *ghayabat* with a doubled consonant (*tashdid*). ﴿Some passing caravan will pick him up﴾ means will take him.

﴿Some of the caravan﴾ means some of those who travel through the land. ﴿If you are going to act﴾ means by my counsel, or if you are going to do what separates him from his father.(p-157)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 11–12:

﴿They said: "O our father, why do you not trust us with Joseph, when we are indeed his sincere well-wishers?"﴾ That is, why do you fear us for him? ﴿And indeed we are truly his sincere well-wishers.﴾ We are compassionate toward him and desire good for him. They intended by this to draw him away from his opinion about guarding him from them, because of what had breathed into them of envy (hasad).

The well-known reading is ﴿ta'manna﴾ with idgham (assimilation of the two identical consonants) with ishmam (a slight indication of the vowel). According to Nafi', it is without ishmam. Among the irregular readings (shawadhdh) is leaving out idgham, because the two words are from two separate words (kalimatayn); and "timan-na" with a kasra on the ta'.

﴿Send him with us tomorrow﴾ to the open country. (Nar'ta') we shall enjoy plenty in eating fruits and the like, from ar-ra'tah (ar-ra'ta), which is abundance (al-khisb).

﴿And let him play﴾ by racing and archery. Ibn Kathir read (narta'i) with a kasra on the ayn, on the basis that it is from irtaa yartaa; and Nafi' (read) with the kasra and the ya' in it and in (yal'ab). The Kufans and Ya'qub read with the ya' and the sukun, on the basis of attributing the verb to Joseph. It has also been read as (yartai') from ar-ta'a mashiyatahu (he pastured his livestock), and (yartai') with a kasra on the ayn, and (yal'abu) with a damma, on the basis of it being a nominal beginning (ibtida').

﴿And indeed we are truly guardians of him﴾ from anything disagreeable befalling him.

He said: "Truly, it grieves me that you take him away," because of the intensity of my separation from him and the weakness of my patience concerning him. "And I fear that the wolf will devour him," because the land was a place of wolves (madh'aba). It was also said that he saw in a dream that a wolf had attacked Joseph, and he was wary of it on his behalf. Ibn Kathir and Nafi' in the transmission of Qalun have hamzated it according to its original form; in the transmission of al-Yazidi, Abu 'Amr when pausing, and 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah when continuing (without pause), it is read without hamza. Its derivation is from "tadha'abat al-rih" (the wind blew from every direction) when it blows from every side. "And you are heedless of him," either because you are occupied with pasturing and play, or because of the little concern you have for guarding him.

They said: "If the wolf devours him while we are a band (usbah)..." The lam here is a preparatory lam (lam muwatta'ah) for the oath, and its answer is: "Indeed we would then be losers," meaning weak and defrauded, or deserving that ruin be invoked upon them. The waw in "wa-nahnu 'usbatun" (while we are a band) is a waw of circumstance (waw al-hal).

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 12, verse 15:**

﴿So when they took him away and agreed to put him into the depths of the well﴾, and they resolved to cast him into it. The well was either the well of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), or a well in the land of al-Urdunn (Jordan), or between Misr (Egypt) and Madyan (Midian), or three farsakh (about nine miles) from the station of Ya'qub (Jacob). The answer to "lamma" (when) is omitted, and its implied meaning is like "they did to him what they did of harm."

It has been narrated that when they brought him out into the desert, they began to harm him and beat him until they nearly killed him. He began to cry out and plead for help, so Yahudha (Judah) said: "Did you not make a covenant with me that you would not kill him?" They brought him to the well and lowered him into it, but he clung to its edge. They tied his hands and stripped off his shirt so that they could smear it with blood and deceive their father with it. He said: "O my brothers, return my shirt to me so that I may cover myself with it." They said: "Call upon the eleven stars, the sun and the moon, and they will clothe you and keep you company." When he reached the middle of the well, they let him fall. There was water in it, so he fell into it, and then he took refuge on a rock that was in it, standing upon it and weeping. Then Jibril (Gabriel) came to him with the revelation, as He says: ﴿And We revealed to him﴾. He was seventeen years old. It is also said that he was an adolescent, and revelation came to him in his youth, just as it came to Yahya (John) and Isa (Jesus), peace be upon them.

In the stories (al-Qasas, the narratives of the prophets) it is related that when Ibrahim (Abraham), peace be upon him, was cast into the fire, he was stripped of his clothes, and Jibril, peace be upon him, brought him a shirt of the silk of Paradise and dressed him in it. Ibrahim passed it to Ishaq (Isaac), and Ishaq passed it to Ya'qub, who placed it in an amulet (tamima) that he hung on Yusuf. Jibril, peace be upon him, took it out and dressed him in it. ﴿You will surely inform them of this affair of theirs﴾: you will surely tell them what they did to you, while they do not perceive that you are Yusuf, because of your high rank, their distance from such imaginings, and the long passage of time that changes appearances and forms. This refers to what he said to them in Misr when they came to him seeking provisions: ﴿So he recognized them, while they did not recognize him﴾. He gave them good news of what his affair would come to, to console him and to comfort his heart. It has also been said that ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ is connected to "We revealed" (awhayna), meaning: We comforted him with revelation while they did not perceive that.

And they came to their father in the early part of the night (ʿishāʾan), that is, at the end of the day. It has also been read as ʿushiyyan, which is a diminutive of ʿashiyy, and ʿushan (with a damma and a short vowel), the plural of aʿshā, meaning that they had become blind from weeping. [They were] weeping, pretending to weep (mutabākīna).

It is narrated that when he heard their weeping, he was alarmed and said: "What is the matter with you, my sons? And where is Yusuf?"

They said: "O our father, we went off racing (nastabiqu), competing with one another in running or in archery. The ifti'āl and tafā'ul forms may share meaning, as in intiḍāl and tanāḍul (both meaning to compete in shooting arrows). And we left Yusuf by our belongings, and the wolf ate him. But you will not believe us (mu'min), not accept our word as truthful, even if we were telling the truth, because of your bad opinion of us and your excessive love for Yusuf."

And they came to their father in the early part of the night (ʿishāʾan), that is, at the end of the day. It has also been read as ʿushiyyan, which is a diminutive of ʿashiyy, and ʿushan (with a damma and a short vowel), the plural of aʿshā, meaning that they had become blind from weeping. [They were] weeping, pretending to weep (mutabākīna).

It is narrated that when he heard their weeping, he was alarmed and said: "What is the matter with you, my sons? And where is Yusuf?"

They said: "O our father, we went off racing (nastabiqu), competing with one another in running or in archery. The ifti'āl and tafā'ul forms may share meaning, as in intiḍāl and tanāḍul (both meaning to compete in shooting arrows). And we left Yusuf by our belongings, and the wolf ate him. But you will not believe us (mu'min), not accept our word as truthful, even if we were telling the truth, because of your bad opinion of us and your excessive love for Yusuf."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 18:

﴿And they came upon his shirt with false blood.﴾ That is, "with blood that is full of falsehood" (dhu kadhib), in the sense of "blood in which there is falsehood" (maktub fihi, i.e., falsely claimed). It is also permissible that it be a description by the verbal noun (al-masdar) for emphasis (al-mubalaghah). It is recited with the accusative (bi'l-nasb) as a circumstantial state (hal) from the waw (of "they came"), meaning "they came lying" (kadhibin). And "kadib" with an unmarked dal (kadib, not dhal) means "turbid" (kadir) or "fresh" (tariyy). It has been said: its origin is the whiteness that emerges on the nails of young children, and blood sticking to the shirt was likened to it. And "upon his shirt" (ala qamisihi) is in the place of the accusative as an adverbial of place (zarf), meaning "above his shirt," or as a circumstantial state (hal) of the blood, if it is permissible to place it before the prepositional phrase.

It is related that when he (Jacob) heard the news of Joseph, he cried out and asked about his shirt. He took it, cast it over his face, and wept until he stained his face with the blood of the shirt, and said: "I have never seen a wolf more gentle than this one, who ate my son and did not tear his shirt."

Therefore he said: ﴿Nay, your souls have made a matter seem fine to you.﴾ That is, your souls made it easy for you and made a great matter trivial in your eyes, from the root sawl, which is relaxation (al-istirkha').

﴿So patience is fitting (sabrun jamil).﴾ That is, "my affair is fitting patience," or "so patience, most fitting (jamil ajmal)." And in a hadith: "Fitting patience is that in which there is no complaint made to the creation."

﴿And Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe.﴾ That is, against bearing what you describe of the destruction of Joseph. And this crime occurred before their prophethood (istinba'ihim), if that is sound.

[Allah says:] ﴿And a caravan came﴾, a company traveling from Midian to Egypt. They stopped near the well, and this was three days after he had been thrown into it.

﴿Then they sent their water-drawer﴾, the one who goes down to the water and draws it for them. He was Malik ibn Dhu'r al-Khuza'i.

﴿So he lowered his bucket﴾ into the well to fill it, and Yusuf clung to it. ﴿When he saw him﴾, he ﴿said: "What good news! This is a boy!"﴾ He called out "bushra" (good news) as a glad tiding for himself or for his people, as if he had said: "Glad tidings! Now is your time." It has also been said that bushra is the name of a companion of his, whom he called to help him bring Yusuf up.

The readers other than the Kufans read «يا بُشْرايَ» ("O my good news!") with the possessive suffix. Hamza and al-Kisa'i pronounced the fatha of the rā' with imala (a fronting of the vowel toward i). Warsh recited between the two forms. It was also read «يا بُشْرى» with idgham (assimilation of the two identical consonants, i.e., merging of the doubled sound), which is a dialectal usage. «يا بُشْرايَ» is also read with sukun (a silent final vowel), intended as a pause (waqf).

﴿And they concealed him﴾, that is, the water-drawer and his companions from the rest of the caravan. It has also been said that they hid his situation and told the others: "The people of the water gave him to us so that we might sell him for them in Egypt." It has also been said that the pronoun refers to Yusuf's brothers, because Yahudha used to bring him food every day. On that day he came to him but did not find him in the well, so he informed his brothers. They went to the caravan and said: "This is our slave who ran away from us, so buy him." Yusuf remained silent for fear that they would kill him.

﴿As merchandise﴾: «بِضاعَةً» is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning they concealed him as a commodity for trade. Its derivation is from al-bid' (a part), since it is a portion of wealth set aside for trade.

﴿And Allah knows well what they do﴾: nothing of their secrets was hidden from Him, or the deed of Yusuf's brothers against their father and their brother.

**﴿And they sold him﴾**, that is, they sold him off. The reference of the pronoun (in "they sold him") admits two possibilities: either it refers to the caravan, or it means "they bought him from his brothers."

**﴿for a paltry price﴾**, that is, a price that was defrauded (*mabkhus*) because it was counterfeit or deficient.

**﴿dirhams﴾** is a substitute (*badal*) for "price."

**﴿counted﴾**, that is, few in number, for they would weigh what reached an *awqiyya* (ounce) and count what was less than that. It has been said that it was twenty dirhams, and it has been said that it was twenty-two dirhams.

**﴿And they were of those who had no interest in him﴾**, that is, those who were averse to him (*al-raghibin 'anhu*). If the pronoun in "they were" refers to the brothers, the meaning is clear. If it refers to the caravan, who were the sellers, then their aversion to him is explained by the fact that they had found him, and one who finds an item treats it lightly, fears having it snatched away, and hastens to sell it. If they were the buyers, then it is because they believed he was a runaway slave. The phrase "concerning him" (*fihi*) is related to "those who had no interest," if the *lam* in *al-zahidin* is taken as the definite article. If the *lam* is taken to mean "the one who" (*alladhi*), then the phrase is related to a deleted element that "those who had no interest" clarifies, because the complement of a relative clause cannot precede the relative pronoun.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 21:

﴿And the one who bought him from Egypt said﴾ He was the ʿAzīz (the chief minister/governor) who was over the treasuries of Egypt, and his name was Qiṭfīr or Iṭfīr. The king at that time was Rayyān ibn al-Walīd al-ʿAmlīqī, and he had believed in Yūsuf, peace be upon him, and died during his lifetime. It is also said that Pharaoh of Moses lived four hundred years, based on the words of the Exalted: ﴿And Yūsuf came to you before with clear proofs﴾. The well-known view is that he was among the descendants of Pharaoh Yūsuf. The verse is of the type of addressing the descendants with the circumstances of their fathers.

It is narrated: he was bought by the ʿAzīz when he was seventeen years old, and he remained in his house for thirteen years, and Rayyān made him his vizier when he was thirty-three years old, and he died when he was one hundred and twenty years old.

There is disagreement about what he was bought for, by those who make his purchase other than the first: twenty dinars, a pair of sandals, and two white garments. It is said his price was filled with silver, and it is said with gold. ﴿To his wife﴾, Rāʿīl or Zulaykhā. ﴿Make his stay honourable﴾, make his position with us honourable, i.e., good, and the meaning is: take good care of him. ﴿Perhaps he will benefit us﴾ in our properties and our wealth, and we will rely on him in our affairs. ﴿Or we may take him as a son﴾, adopting him; he was barren, because of what he perceived in him of right judgment. For this reason it was said: the three most perceptive of people were the ʿAzīz of Egypt, the daughter of Shuʿayb who said ﴿O my father, hire him﴾, and Abū Bakr when he appointed ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both. ﴿And thus We established Yūsuf in the land﴾, just as We established his love in the heart of the ʿAzīz, or just as We settled him in his house, or just as We rescued him and inclined the ʿAzīz toward him, We established him therein. ﴿And that We may teach him the interpretation of events﴾ is conjoined to an implied clause whose estimate is: so that he may act with justice therein; and "that We may teach him" means the purpose of his rescue and establishment was that he would establish justice and manage the affairs of people, and know the meanings of the Books of Allah the Exalted and His rulings so that he would implement them; or the interpretation of dreams, which alert to events that will occur, so that he may prepare for them and occupy himself with managing them before they arrive, as he did for his years. ﴿And Allah is dominant over His affair﴾, nothing repels it and none contends with Him in what He wills; or over the affair of Yūsuf: his brothers intended something against him, and Allah intended other than it, so nothing happened except what He willed. ﴿But most of the people do not know﴾ that the whole matter is in His hand, or the subtleties of His workmanship and the hidden aspects of His kindness.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 22:

﴿And when he reached his maturity﴾: the limit of the strengthening of his body and his power, and it is the age of standing firm (sinn al-wuquf), which is between thirty and forty. It is also said that it is the age of youth (sinn al-shabab), whose beginning is the attainment of puberty (bulugh al-hulm).

﴿We gave him judgement﴾: wisdom (hikmah), which is knowledge supported by action; or a judge (hakam) among the people.

﴿And knowledge﴾: meaning the knowledge of the interpretation of events (ta'wil al-ahadith). ﴿Thus do We reward the good-doers﴾: an indication that Allah, exalted is He, gave him that only as a reward for his goodness in his work and his excellence in the prime of his affairs (p-160).

﴿And she, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him from himself﴾. She asked him and contrived to get him to lie with her. The verb is from *rāda yarūdu*, meaning to come and go in search of something, and from it comes *al-rāʾid* (the scout).

﴿And she bolted the doors﴾. It is said there were seven of them. The doubling of the letter in *ghallaqat* indicates multiplicity or emphasis in securing them.

﴿And she said, "Come, you"﴾. That is, "Come on, and hasten," or, "I have prepared myself." On both readings, *hayta* is an *ism fiʿl* (a verb-noun, a noun functioning as a verb), built on fatḥa like *ayna*, and the *lām* in *laka* is for clarification, as in *suqyan laka*.

Ibn Kathīr read it with a ḍamma and with a fatḥa on the *hāʾ*, likening it to *ḥayth* (where). Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read it with a fatḥa and a kasra on the *hāʾ*, like *ʿiṭ*. Hishām read it the same way but with a hamza. It is also narrated from him that he read the *tāʾ* with a ḍamma, which is a dialect form of it. It was also read *hīt*, like *jīr*, and *hiʾtu*, like *jiʾtu*, from *hāʾa yahīʾu* when one prepares oneself. It was read *huyyiʾtu*, and on this reading the *lām* belongs to its complement.

﴿He said, "God forbid"﴾. That is, "I seek refuge in God, a seeking of refuge."

﴿Indeed, he﴾: that is, indeed the matter. ﴿My Lord has made my lodging good﴾: my master Qiṭfīr has treated me well, since he said to you about me, ﴿Make his stay honorable﴾. So what would be the recompense for him if I betrayed him in his household? It is also said that the pronoun refers to God Most High, meaning: "Indeed He, my Creator, has made my station good, by being kind to my heart, so that I will not disobey Him."

﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers do not prosper﴾: those who repay good with evil. It is also said they are adulterers, since adultery is an injustice both to the adulterer and to the one he violates in his family.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 24:

﴿And indeed she desired him, and he would have desired her﴾. She aimed at intimacy with him, and he aimed at intimacy with her. Al-hamm (intention, resolve) toward a thing is aiming at it and resolving upon it; from it comes al-humam (the resolute man), who is one who, when he resolves upon a thing, carries it through. What is meant by his desire, peace be upon him, is the inclination of nature and the struggle of appetite, not a deliberate, chosen intention. This is not something that falls under legal obligation; rather, the one deserving of praise and of a great reward from God is the one who restrains himself from the act when this desire arises, or when it approaches, as when you say, "I would have killed him, had I not feared God."

﴿Had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾: in the ugliness of fornication and the evil of its consequence, he would have had intimacy with her, out of the intensity of sexual urge and the extreme of insistence. It is not permissible to make ﴿and he desired her﴾ the response (jawab) of ﴿had it not been﴾ (lawla), for lawla is in the rule of conditional particles, so its response does not precede it; rather, the response is omitted and is indicated by what precedes it. It was said: he saw Gabriel, peace be upon him. It was said: Jacob appeared to him, biting on his fingertips. It was said: Qitfir. It was said: he was called, "O Joseph, you are written among the prophets, and you act the deeds of the foolish."

﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like that steadfastness, We made him steadfast; or, the matter is like that. ﴿That We might turn away from him evil﴾: the betrayal of the master. ﴿And immorality﴾: fornication. ﴿Indeed he was of Our sincere servants﴾: those whom God purified for His obedience. Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, Ibn Amir and Ya'qub read with kasra in the whole Qur'an whenever the definite article (al-) is at its beginning, i.e., "those who made their religion sincere for God" (mukhlisin, with the kasra on the lam of the verb's active form: al-mukhlisina being read as al-mukhlisina with the active sense).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 25:

﴿And they both raced to the door﴾ i.e., they raced one another to the door, so the preposition has been omitted, or the verb has been construed to carry the sense of hastening (ibtidar) [a technical term meaning "rushing to take the initiative"]. That is because Yusuf fled from her in order to go out, and she hurried after him to prevent him from going out. ﴿And she tore his shirt from the back﴾: she pulled it from behind him, so his shirt was torn. The qadd is a tear lengthwise, and the qatt is a tear crosswise. ﴿And they found her husband﴾: they came upon her husband. ﴿At the door. She said: What is the recompense for one who intended evil for your wife, except that he be imprisoned or suffer a painful punishment?﴾ [She said this] giving the impression that she had fled from him, to clear her own name before her husband and to turn him against Yusuf and incite him against him out of a desire for revenge. The ma here is either negating (nafiyah) or interrogative (istifhamiyyah) in the sense of "what," [meaning:] what is the recompense for him, other than prison?(p-161)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 26–27:

﴿He said: "It was she who sought to seduce me away from myself."﴾ She demanded of me compliance. He said this only to repel what she had exposed him to of imprisonment or a painful punishment, and had he not been lying about him he would not have said it. ﴿And a witness from her own family testified.﴾ It was said: a paternal cousin of hers. It was also said: a maternal cousin of hers, an infant in the cradle.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Four spoke while still infants: the son of Pharaoh's hairdresser, the witness of Joseph, the companion of Jurayj, and Jesus son of Mary, upon him be peace." God placed the testimony on the tongue of one of her family only so that it would be more binding upon her. ﴿If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has spoken truly and he is among the liars.﴾ Because it indicates that she tore his shirt from in front of him in pushing him away from herself, or that he rushed after her, stumbled on his garment, and his collar was torn.

﴿And if his shirt is torn from the back, then she has lied and he is among the truthful.﴾ Because it indicates that she followed him, seized his garment, and tore it.

The conditional clause is reported in the sense of the verb "saying," or because the act of testifying is a form of speech. It is called a testimony because it performed its function. The combination of "in" (إنْ) and "kana" (كانَ) is understood in the sense that it is known that he "was" and the like. A parallel is your saying: "If you have done good to me until today, then I have done good to you before," meaning: if you bestow on me your present kindness, I bestow on you my earlier kindness.

The words "min qubulin" (مِن قُبُلٍ) and "min dubурin" (مِن دُبُرٍ) are read with a ḍamma, because both have been cut off from the genitive construction, like "qablu" (قَبْلُ) and "ba'du" (بَعْدُ); and with a fatḥa, as if they were made proper names for the two directions, so that they are not declined; and with a sukūn on the ʿayn.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verses 28–29:

﴿So when he saw his shirt torn from behind, he said: Indeed, it is﴾ — that is, your saying — ﴿"What is the recompense for one who intended harm to your family, except that he be imprisoned or subjected to a painful punishment?"﴾ — or, "indeed, the evil" or "indeed, this matter." ﴿"Of your guile (kaid)."﴾ — of your deceit (hilah), and the address is to her and to those like her, or to women in general. ﴿"Indeed, your guile is great."﴾ For the guile of women is more subtle, more adhering to the heart, and more forceful in its effect upon the soul; and because they confront men with it, while Satan whispers it covertly.

﴿"Joseph"﴾ — the vocative particle has been omitted from it, due to his nearness and his alertness to the conversation. ﴿"Turn away from this"﴾ — conceal it and do not mention it.

﴿"And ask forgiveness for your sin"﴾ — O Ra'il (Ra'ila). ﴿"Indeed, you were of those who erred."﴾ — of the sinning people; from khati'a, when one sins deliberately; and the masculine form is used for the sake of predominance (al-taghlib).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verses 28–29:

﴿So when he saw his shirt torn from behind, he said: Indeed, it is﴾ — that is, your saying — ﴿"What is the recompense for one who intended harm to your family, except that he be imprisoned or subjected to a painful punishment?"﴾ — or, "indeed, the evil" or "indeed, this matter." ﴿"Of your guile (kaid)."﴾ — of your deceit (hilah), and the address is to her and to those like her, or to women in general. ﴿"Indeed, your guile is great."﴾ For the guile of women is more subtle, more adhering to the heart, and more forceful in its effect upon the soul; and because they confront men with it, while Satan whispers it covertly.

﴿"Joseph"﴾ — the vocative particle has been omitted from it, due to his nearness and his alertness to the conversation. ﴿"Turn away from this"﴾ — conceal it and do not mention it.

﴿"And ask forgiveness for your sin"﴾ — O Ra'il (Ra'ila). ﴿"Indeed, you were of those who erred."﴾ — of the sinning people; from khati'a, when one sins deliberately; and the masculine form is used for the sake of predominance (al-taghlib).

**﴿And women said﴾** *Niswatun* (نِسْوَةٌ) is a collective noun (*ism*) for the plural of *imra'ah* (امْرَأةٌ). Its feminine marking in this sense is not a true (*ḥaqīqī*) feminine, and for this reason its verb is left unmarked for gender (*jurrida fi'luhu*). Pronouncing the *nūn* with a *ḍammah* (نُسْوَةٌ) is a dialectal variant (*lughah*) of the word.

**﴿in the city﴾** This is an adverb of place (*ẓarf*) governing *qāla* (said), meaning: they spread the report in Egypt (*miṣr*). Alternatively, it is an adjective (*ṣifah*) of *niswah*.

They were five women: the wife of the chamberlain (*ḥājib*), the wife of the cupbearer (*sāqī*), the wife of the baker (*khabbāz*), the wife of the jailer (*sajjān*), and the wife of the keeper of the animals (*ṣāḥib al-dawābb*).

**﴿The wife of al-'Aziz is seeking to seduce her young man from himself﴾** She seeks to have intercourse (*muwāqa'ah*) with her slave-boy (*ghulām*), who is her servant.

*Al-'Azīz* in the language of the Arabs means the king. The root of *fatan* (فَتًى, young man) is *fatiya* (فَتِيَ), as shown by their plural *fityān* (فِتْيانٌ). The noun *al-futuwwah* (فُتُوَّةٌ, youthfulness/chivalry) is an irregular (*shādh*) form.

**﴿She has certainly been overcome with love for him﴾** *Shaqqa shaghāfa qalbihā*, meaning he pierced the *shaghāf* of her heart, which is its covering (*ḥijābuhu*), until it reached her heart (*fu'ād*) with love. The word *ḥubban* (حُبًّا) is in the accusative of specification (*tamyīz*), used to divert the action (*ṣarf al-fi'l*) away from its subject. It has also been read as *sha'afahā* (شَعَفَها), from *sha'afa al-ba'īr*, meaning he smeared the camel with tar and burned it.

**﴿Indeed, we see her in manifest error﴾** She is in error (*ḍalāl*) away from right guidance (*rushd*) and far from what is correct (*ṣawāb*).

(p-162) ﴿When she heard of their scheming﴾, that is, of their backbiting. He called it scheming because they concealed it, as a schemer conceals his scheme; or they said that so that she would show them Yusuf; or because she had entrusted them with her secret and they disclosed it about her. ﴿She sent for them﴾, inviting them. It is said she invited forty women, among whom were the five mentioned. ﴿And prepared for them a couch﴾, that is, what they would recline upon of cushions. ﴿And gave each one of them a knife﴾, so that they would recline while the knives were in their hands; then when he came out to them they would be struck dumb and occupied away from themselves, so that their hands would fall upon their hands and they would cut them, and thus they would be rebuked by the proof. Or Yusuf, when he came out alone to forty women with daggers in their hands, would fear their scheming. It is also said that ﴿muttaka'﴾ means food, or a place of food, for they used to recline for food and drink out of luxury, and for this it was forbidden. Jamil said:

﴿So we remained in blessing and reclined, and drank the lawful from its jugs﴾

It is also said that al-muttaka' is food that is cut into pieces, as if the cutter leans upon it with the knife. It was recited as "muttakan" with the hamza omitted, and "muttaka'an" with the fatha lengthened, like "muntazahin"; and "muttakan," which is the citron, or what is cut off from "mataka al-shay'" when one severs it; and "muttakaan" from "taka'a," "yuttaka'u," when one reclines. ﴿And she said, "Come out before them." So when they saw him, they magnified him﴾, glorified him, and were awed by his surpassing beauty.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "I saw Yusuf on the night of the Ascension like the moon on the night of the full moon." It is also said that his face's radiance used to be seen reflected on the walls. It is also said that ﴿akbarna﴾ means "menstruated," from "akbarat al-mar'ah" when she menstruated, because she enters into maturity (kibar) through menstruation; the pronoun "ha'" refers to the verbal noun or to Yusuf, peace be upon him, with the lam omitted, meaning they menstruated on account of him, from the intensity of lust, as al-Mutanabbi said:

﴿Fear God, and veil this beauty with a face-veil, for if you appear, the unmarried girls in their chambers menstruate﴾

﴿And they cut their hands﴾, wounding them with the knives, out of extreme bewilderment. ﴿And they said, "Hasha lillah!"﴾, declaring God free of attributes of incapacity and marveling at His power to create the like of him. Its origin is "hasha," as Abu 'Amr recited in continuous speech, its final alif being dropped for lightness. It is a particle that conveys the meaning of exoneration in the context of exception, so it was placed in the position of exoneration, and the lam is for specification, as in your saying "suqyan laka" (watering to you). 

It was recited "Hasha Allahu" without the lam, meaning "the innocence of God," and "Hashan lillah" with tanwin, treating it as a verbal noun. It is also said that "hasha" is an active participle from "al-hasha," which is the side, and its agent is a pronoun referring to Yusuf, meaning he has come to the side of God from what is suspected of him. ﴿"This is not a human!"﴾, because this beauty is not customary among humans. It is in the Hijazi dialect, applying to it the function of "laysa," for it shares with it the negation of the present state.

It was recited "basharun" with the nominative, in the dialect of Tamim, and "bishra," meaning "a purchased slave of base lineage." ﴿"This is none but a noble angel"﴾, for the combination of pleasing beauty, surpassing perfection, and utmost sinlessness is among the distinguishing qualities of angels; or because his beauty exceeds human beauty, and none surpasses it except an angel.

She said, "That is the one you blamed me for. I did indeed try to seduce him, but he refused. And if he does not do what I order him, he will certainly be imprisoned and will be among the humiliated."

Translation of the commentary:

"She said, 'That is the one about whom you blamed me.'" That is: "So this is the Canaanite slave about whom you blamed me for being infatuated with him before you had truly conceived of him. Had you conceived of him as you have now seen him, you would have excused me." Or it means: "This is the one about whom you blamed me," and "that" is placed in the position of "this," to elevate the rank of the one being pointed to.

"And indeed I sought to seduce him, but he refused." That is, he abstained, seeking chastity. She confessed to them when she realized that they would excuse her, so that they would help her in softening his disposition.

"And if he does not do what I command him." That is, what I command him to do, so the preposition is omitted; or "my commanding him" in the sense of "the thing that makes my command binding," in which case the pronoun refers to Yusuf.

"He will certainly be imprisoned and will be among the humiliated." Min al-saghirin: from the abject. It is from saghira (with kasra), yasghuru, sighran and sagharan, and al-saghir from saghura (with damma), sughran. It is also read "layakunanna," which contradicts the orthography of the Mushaf, because the nun was written in it with an alif, as in "nasfa'an," according to the rule of pause; and this applies to the light (khafifa) nun, because of its resemblance to tanwin.

(p-163) ﴿Said he: "My Lord, prison is dearer to me than what they invite me to.”﴾ Ya'qub (Yaʿqub) read it with a fatha (السِّجْنُ as al-saj(a)n), taking it as a verbal noun (maṣdar). ﴿Dearer to me than what they invite me to﴾, i.e., more preferable to me than yielding to them in fornication, looking to the outcome, even though that is something the soul desires and this is something it dislikes. The attribution of the invitation to them all collectively is because they threatened him for disobeying her and made obedience to her attractive to him. Or, they invited him to themselves. It was said that he was afflicted with prison because of this statement, and it would have been better for him to ask God for well-being; for this reason, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) rebuked the one who asked for patience. ﴿And unless You turn away from me﴾, i.e., if You do not turn away from me, ﴿their scheme﴾, in making that beloved to me and beautifying it in my eyes, by keeping me steadfast in chastity. ﴿I may incline toward them﴾, i.e., I may lean toward their side, or toward themselves, by my natural disposition and the demands of my desire. Ṣabwa (ṣabwah) is inclination toward desire, and from it comes ṣabā (the east wind), because souls find it pleasant and incline toward it. It was also read as ﴿aṣbu﴾ from ṣabāba (ṣabāba), which means longing. ﴿And I would be among the ignorant﴾, i.e., among the foolish, by committing what they invite me to, for the wise do not do what is ugly; or, among those who do not act upon what they know, for they and the ignorant are alike.

﴿So his Lord responded to him﴾: God answered his supplication, which was contained in his saying: ﴿unless You turn away﴾. ﴿So He turned away from him their scheme﴾: He kept him steadfast with chastity until he resolved himself to the hardship of prison and preferred it over the pleasure that entails disobedience. ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing﴾ of the supplication of those who seek refuge in Him, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of their states and what sets them right.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 35–36:

﴿Then it occurred to them, after they had seen the signs,﴾ then it became apparent to the Chieftain (al-'Aziz) and his household, after they had seen the indications that proved Yusuf's innocence: such as the testimony of the infant, the tearing of the shirt from behind, and the women cutting their hands, and his steadfastness (istis'am) against them. The subject of "badā" (it occurred) is an implied pronoun, which is explained by what follows. ﴿that they should imprison him for a while.﴾ This was because she (the wife) deceived her husband and induced him to imprison him for a period, until she could see what would become of him, or until people would suppose that he was the wrongdoer. So he remained in prison for seven years. It is also read with the letter "tā'" (tusjununnahu), on the basis that some speakers addressed it to the Chieftain as a form of honour, or to the Chieftain and those around him. And "ḥattā" (ʿattā) is in the dialect of Hudhayl.

﴿And there entered the prison with him two young men.﴾ That is, Yusuf was taken into the prison, and it happened that two others from the servants of the King, his cupbearer and his baker, were brought in at that time, on the charge that they intended to poison him. ﴿One of them said⦁﴾ meaning the cupbearer. ﴿"Indeed I see myself"⦁﴾ that is, in a dream, and this is the narration of a past state. ﴿"pressing wine"⦁﴾ that is, grapes, and he called them wine by considering what they will become. ﴿And the other said⦁﴾ that is, the baker. ﴿"Indeed I see myself carrying bread upon my head, of which the birds eat"⦁﴾ pecking at it. ﴿"Inform us of its interpretation; indeed we see you as one of the good-doers"⦁﴾ among those who excel in interpreting dreams, or among the knowledgeable. They said this because they had seen him in the prison reminding people and interpreting their dreams; or [it means] among the good-doers toward the people of the prison, so be good to us by interpreting what we have seen, if you know it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verses 37–38:

﴿He said: "No food will come to you as provision but I shall inform you of its interpretation before it comes to you. That is part of what my Lord has taught me."﴾ That is, of the interpretation of what you two have related to me; or, of the interpretation of the food, meaning the explanation of its essence and its manner, for it resembles the explanation of an obscure matter. It is as if he intended to call them to monotheism (tawhid) and guide them to the straight path before he answered what they had asked of him, as is the practice of the prophets and of the scholars who occupy their stations in guidance and direction. So he put first what would be a miracle for him, namely the report of the unseen, so that it would show them his truthfulness in the call and in the interpretation. ﴿Before there comes to you that [interpretation]﴾, that is, that interpretation. ﴿Of what my Lord has taught me﴾, through inspiration and revelation, and it is not of the kind of soothsaying (takahhun) or astrology (tanjim). ﴿Indeed, I have abandoned the creed of a people who do not believe in God and who are disbelievers in the Hereafter﴾: this is a justification for what precedes it, that is, He taught me that because I have abandoned the creed of those people.

﴿And I follow the creed of my forefathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob﴾. Or it is a new statement, introduced to prepare the call and to show that he is from the house of prophethood, so that their desire to listen to him and to trust in him would grow. For this reason it is permitted for one who carries knowledge to describe himself so that he may be recognized and his knowledge may be learned from him. The repetition of the pronoun serves to indicate their exclusiveness and to emphasize their disbelief in the Hereafter. ﴿It is not for us﴾, that is, it is not proper for us, the company of prophets, ﴿to associate anything with God﴾, whatever it may be. ﴿That﴾, that is, monotheism, ﴿is of God's bounty upon us﴾, through revelation. ﴿And upon mankind﴾, and upon all mankind, in that He sends us to guide them and to keep them firm upon it. ﴿But most people﴾, those to whom we are sent, ﴿do not give thanks﴾ for this bounty, so they turn away from it and do not heed it. Or, it is of God's bounty upon us and upon them, through the establishing of proofs and the sending down of signs, but most of them do not look at these nor reason by them, so they disregard them, like one who denies a blessing and does not give thanks for it.

O two companions of the prison! (﴿يا صاحِبَيِ السِّجْنِ﴾) That is, O you who dwell in it, or O my two companions in it. He attributed them to the prison by way of *ittisa'* (a figurative broadening of speech), as in his saying:

*"O stealer of the night, (you) people of the house!"*

﴿Are scattered lords better﴾ (﴿أأرْبابٌ مُتَفَرِّقُونَ﴾), meaning many, diverse, and multiple, equal in their footing (*mutasawiyat al-aqdam*), ﴿or God, the One﴾ (﴿اللَّهُ الواحِدُ﴾), who is singular in divinity (*uluhiyya*), ﴿the Subduer﴾ (﴿القَهّارُ﴾), the Dominant, to whom none is equal and whom none can resist.

﴿What you worship besides Him﴾ (﴿ما تَعْبُدُونَ مِن دُونِهِ﴾) is addressed to the two of them and to those of Egypt who follow their religion. ﴿Are but names you have named, you and your fathers, for which God has sent down no authority﴾ (﴿إلا أسْماءً سَمَّيْتُمُوها أنْتُمْ وآباؤُكم ما أنْزَلَ اللَّهُ بِها مِن سُلْطانٍ﴾). That is, they are only things considered in terms of names you have applied to them without any proof establishing that their named realities are actually present in them. So it is as if you worship nothing but bare names. The meaning is that you named what neither reason nor transmitted revelation indicates deserves divinity as "gods," and then you began to worship them on account of the names you attach to them.

﴿The judgment is not but for God﴾ (﴿إنِ الحُكْمُ إلا لِلَّهِ﴾), meaning that the decision regarding worship belongs to none but Him, ﴿because He is the One who deserves it essentially﴾, since He is the Necessary Being in Himself (*wajib li-dhatihi*), the Originator of all, and the Owner of its affair. ﴿He has commanded﴾ (﴿أمَرَ﴾) through His prophets ﴿that you worship none but Him﴾ (﴿ألا تَعْبُدُوا إلا إيّاهُ﴾), the One whom the proofs indicate. ﴿That is the upright religion﴾ (﴿ذَلِكَ الدِّينُ القَيِّمُ﴾), the truth, ﴿but most people do not know﴾ (﴿وَلَكِنَّ أكْثَرَ النّاسِ لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾), and you do not distinguish the crooked from the straight.

This is part of the gradual method of da'wah (call to faith) and of establishing proof. He first showed them, by way of persuasion (*khitaba*), the superiority of tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness) over taking other gods. Then he demonstrated that what they call gods and worship does not deserve divinity, for the right to worship is either essential or derived from another, and both are absent from them. Then he explicitly stated the true, upright truth and the straight religion, which reason does not require beyond it and knowledge does not accept in place of it. ﴿But most people do not know﴾, and so they stumble about in their ignorance.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 42:

﴿And he said to the one of the two whom he thought would be saved: "Mention me to your lord."﴾ The one who thought (zann) was Yusuf. If he mentioned this on the basis of ijtihad (independent reasoning), then he is the one who will be saved; but if he mentioned it on the basis of revelation, then the zann is to be interpreted as certainty (yaqin).

﴿"Mention me to your lord"﴾: mention my condition to the king, so that he may release me.

﴿But Satan caused him to forget the mention of his lord﴾: so the cupbearer forgot to mention him to his lord. The verbal noun (masdar) is attributed to him because he is connected with it, or it is taken as meaning "the report of his lord" (dhikr akhbar rabbihi). Or it means that Yusuf was caused to forget the remembrance of God, so that he sought help from other than Him. This is supported by the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "May God have mercy on my brother Yusuf. Had he not said, ﴿Mention me to your lord﴾, he would not have remained in prison seven years after the five."

Seeking help from people in removing hardships, although praiseworthy in general, is not befitting the rank of the prophets.

﴿So he remained in prison for several years﴾: al-bid' (bid') is what lies between three and nine, from bid' (bid'), which means "cutting off."

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 12, verses 43–44**

﴿And the king said, "Indeed, I see seven fat cows being devoured by seven lean ones."⁠﴾ When his release drew near, the king saw seven fat cows coming out of a dry river, and seven lean cows, and the lean ones swallowed the fat ones. ﴿And seven green ears of grain﴾: their grain had already formed. ﴿And [seven] others, dry﴾: and seven other dry ones, which had ripened. The dry ears wound around the green ones until they overcame them. He dispensed with describing their condition because of what had already been related about the condition of the cows, and he made the fat ones agree with the thing being specified (al-mumayyaz) rather than the specifier (al-mumayyiz), because the specification was made by them. He described the second group of seven as ﴿lean﴾ because it is impossible to specify them by themselves, separated from the thing described, for it serves to indicate the kind. Its analogical plural would be ʿujuf, since it is the plural of ʿajfa'. But it was treated as if it were sim̄an, because it is the opposite of that word.

﴿O you chiefs, give me your opinion concerning my vision﴾: interpret it. ﴿If you are able to interpret visions﴾: if you are knowledgeable in the expression of visions. Interpreting a vision (ʿibarat al-ru'ya) is the movement from imaginative forms to the inner meanings they resemble, and it is taken from ʿubur (crossing over), which means passing beyond. One says ʿabbartu al-ru'ya ʿibara, which is more emphatic than ʿabbartuha taʿbiran. The lam is either for specification (lil-bayan) or to strengthen the governing verb, since when the verb is placed after its object it becomes weaker and is therefore strengthened by the lam, as with the active participle. Or it may be because taʿburun includes the meaning of a verb that takes the lam as its complement, as if it were said: "If you are appointed for the interpretation of visions."

﴿They said, "These are confused dreams."⁠﴾ That is, this is a confusion of dreams. The word (ḍighth) is singular, and its root is what is gathered of mixed plants and bundles, and so it is used metaphorically for a false vision. They used the plural form for the sake of emphasizing the falsehood of the dream, as when they say: "So-and-so rides horses," or because it includes various different things. ﴿And we are not versed in the interpretation of dreams⁠﴾: they mean by "dreams" specifically the false dreams, that is, they have no interpretation according to us. Interpretation (taʾwil) applies only to true dreams. This is, as it were, a second premise offered as an excuse for their ignorance of its interpretation.

﴿O you chiefs, give me your opinion concerning my vision﴾: interpret it. ﴿If you are able to interpret visions﴾: if you are knowledgeable in the expression of visions. The lam is either for specification (lil-bayan) or to strengthen the governing verb, since when the verb is placed after its object it becomes weaker and is therefore strengthened by the lam, as with the active participle. ﴿They said, "These are confused dreams."⁠﴾ That is, this is a confusion of dreams. The word (ḍighth) is singular, and its root is what is gathered of mixed plants and bundles, and so it is used metaphorically for a false vision. They used the plural form for the sake of emphasizing the falsehood of the dream, as when they say: "So-and-so rides horses," or because it includes various different things. ﴿And we are not versed in the interpretation of dreams⁠﴾: they mean by "dreams" specifically the false dreams, that is, they have no interpretation according to us. Interpretation (taʾwil) applies only to true dreams. This is, as it were, a second premise offered as an excuse for their ignorance of its interpretation.

﴿And the one of the two who was saved from them said﴾, namely the one of the two prisoners, who was the cupbearer. ﴿and he remembered after a long time﴾. He recalled Yusuf after a group of time-periods had gathered, meaning a long duration. It is read as «إمَّةٍ» (*immatin*) with a kasra on the hamza, which means a blessing, that is, after he had been granted deliverance. It is also read as «أُمَّهْ» (*ummah*), meaning forgetfulness. One says أمَهَ يَأْمَهُ أمَهًا (*amaha ya'mahu amahan*) when someone forgets. The clause is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraḍ*, a clause placed between parts of a sentence), and what follows is the content of the saying. ﴿I will inform you of its interpretation, so send me forth﴾, that is, to the one who has its knowledge, or to the prison.

He did not make his statement conclusive regarding these two matters because he was not certain of returning, so perhaps he would die before that and would not inform them.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verses 47–49:**

﴿He said: "You will sow for seven years, consistently"﴾. That is, according to your continuous custom. Its being in the accusative (intisab) is as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning "persevering" (da'ibin), or as a verbal noun (masdar) with its verb omitted, i.e., "you will persevere with perseverance (da'ban)," and the sentence would then be a circumstantial clause. Hafs read "da'aban" with a fatha on the hamza, and both forms are verbal nouns of da'aba in work (da'aba fi al-'amal). It was also said that "tazra'una" is an imperative, which he expressed in the form of a declarative statement for emphasis, in keeping with His words: ﴿So what you reap, leave it in its ear﴾, lest the weevil eat it. According to the first reading, this is advice outside the literal wording. ﴿Except a little of what you eat﴾ in those years.

﴿Then after that there will come seven hard years which will consume what you have stored up for them﴾. That is, they will consume what you have saved for their sake; the act was attributed to them figuratively (majaz), so as to match between the one who interprets and the thing interpreted. ﴿Except a little of what you guard﴾, that is, what you set aside as seed for planting.

﴿Then after that there will come a year in which the people will be given rain (yughathu al-nas)﴾, that is, they will be rained upon, from ghayth (rain), or they will be relieved from drought, from ghawth (relief).

﴿And in it they will press (ya'sirun)﴾, that is, what is pressed, such as grapes and olives, because of the abundance of fruits. It was also said that they will milk the udders. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with the letter ta' (ta'sirun), by way of giving precedence to the addressees. It was also read in the passive form from 'asara-hu, meaning "to deliver him"; and it may be that the active form from it is intended, i.e., God will relieve them and they will relieve one another; or it is from a'sarat al-sahabatu 'alayhim (the cloud brought rain upon them), in which case the object is transitive by removing the preposition or by implying the meaning of rain.

This is good news, which he gave them after he had interpreted the fat cows and the green ears of grain as years of abundance, and the lean cows and the dry ears as years of drought, and the devouring of the lean ones of the fat ones as the consumption, during the years of drought, of what had been gathered during the years of abundance. Perhaps he knew this by revelation, or because the end of drought is with abundance, or because the divine custom is to widen provision for His servants after having constricted it for them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 50:

﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me."﴾ After the messenger had come to him with the interpretation, and when the messenger came to bring him out. ﴿He said, "Return to your lord and ask him what was the matter with the women who cut their hands."﴾ He delayed going out and put first the questioning of the women and the examination of their condition, so that his innocence would become manifest and it would be known that he had been imprisoned unjustly, and so that the envier could not use him as a means to disparage his affair. In this is evidence that one should strive to negate accusations and avoid the places where they occur.

And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "If I had been in his place and had remained in prison as long as he remained, I would have hastened to answer." He said ﴿ask him what was the matter with the women﴾ and did not say "ask him to investigate their condition," urging him to search and to establish the truth of the matter. He did not mention his mistress despite what she had done to him, out of generosity and observance of good manners. It has also been read "al-Nuswah" with a ḍammah on the nūn. ﴿Indeed my Lord is Knowing of their plot﴾ when they said to me, "Obey your mistress." In this is the magnification of their plot, the invoking of God's knowledge as a witness to it and to his innocence of what he was accused of, and a warning to them for their plotting.

(p-167) ﴿He said, "What was your affair, when you sought to seduce Joseph from himself?"﴾ The king said to them, "What is your matter?" *Al-khatb* (the matter, affair) is a thing that its owner has a right to be addressed about. ﴿They said, "Hasha lillah (God forbid)! We know of him no evil."﴾ *Hasha lillah* is a declaration of God's transcendence and a marvelling at His power to create a chaste person like him. ﴿"No evil"﴾ means no sin. ﴿The wife of al-Aziz said, "Now the truth has become evident."﴾ *Hasössa* (became established and settled), from *hasḥasa al-ba'īr*, when the camel casts down its chest so that it may kneel. The poet said:

*So its knees settled on the hard rocks, and it knelt down with Salma's riders, then grew still.*

Or it means "appeared," from *hassa sha'rahu*, when he shaved off his hair so that the skin of his head appeared. It is also recited in the passive form. ﴿"It was I who sought to seduce him from himself, and he is indeed among the truthful."﴾ This refers to her saying: ﴿"It was she who sought to seduce me from myself."﴾ ﴿"That is so that he may know,"﴾ said by Joseph when the messenger returned to him and informed him of their words. That is, this verification is so that al-Aziz may know ﴿"that I did not betray him in his absence,"﴾ *bil-ghayb* (in absence). The phrase *bi-zahr al-ghayb* means "behind his back," and it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of either the subject or the object: I did not betray him while I was absent from him, or he was absent from me. Alternatively, *bil-ghayb* is an adverb of place, meaning in the place of absence, behind the curtains and the closed doors. ﴿"And that God does not guide the scheming of the treacherous,"﴾ meaning He does not make it succeed or prosper. Or it means He does not guide the treacherous in their scheming, and the verb is attributed to the scheming for emphasis. In this there is an implicit allusion to Ra'il (Potiphar's wife) in her betrayal of her husband, and an affirmation of Joseph's trustworthiness. For this reason he followed it with the words:

**Al-Baydawi's commentary (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 12, verse 53:**

﴿Nor do I absolve myself﴾, meaning I do not declare myself pure, to make clear that he did not intend by this to praise himself or to take pride in his own state, but rather to display the protection (*'ismah*) and divine success (*tawfiq*) that God had bestowed on him.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that when [Yusuf] said, ﴿so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾, Jibril said to him, "Nor when you were inclined [to her]," and so he said that. ﴿Indeed, the soul is certainly a commander to evil﴾, insofar as it is by nature inclined towards desires, so it desires them, and it employs the faculties and the limbs in pursuit of them at all times. ﴿Except those upon whom my Lord has mercy﴾, that is, except at the time of my Lord's mercy, or except those souls whom God has shown mercy to, so that He protects them from that.

It has been said that the exception is disconnected (*istithna' munqati'*), meaning: but the mercy of my Lord is what turns away the evil. It has also been said that the verse is a quotation of the words of Ra'il, and that the exception refers to Yusuf himself and those like him.

It is related from Ibn Kathir and Nafi' that they read (*bi-s-suwwi*) with the hamza changed into a waw (*qalb al-hamzah waw*), then assimilated (*idgham*) into the following letter. ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving, Merciful﴾: He forgives the inclination of the soul, and has mercy on whom He wills through protection. Or [it means] He forgives the one who seeks forgiveness for his sin and confesses against himself, and has mercy on him, for what he sought forgiveness and mercy for, from what he committed.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 54:

﴿And the king said: Bring him to me; I will take him for myself.﴾ I will make him exclusively for myself. ﴿So when he had spoken with him﴾ i.e., when they brought him and he spoke with him, and he witnessed from him right judgment (rushd) and shrewdness (dahaa'). ﴿He said: Indeed, you are today firmly established (makin) with us,﴾ possessing rank and standing. ﴿Trustworthy (amin).﴾ Entrusted with everything.

It is narrated that when he came out of the prison, he bathed, cleansed himself, and put on new garments. When he entered upon the king, he said: "O Allah, I ask You for its good, and I seek refuge in Your might and Your power from its evil." Then he greeted him and supplicated for him in Hebrew (al-'ibriyyah). The king said: "What is this tongue?" He said: "The tongue of my forefathers." The king knew seventy tongues, so he spoke to him in them, and he answered him in all of them, and the king marvelled at him. He said: "I would like to hear my dream from you." So he related it, and described to him the cows and the ears of grain and their places as he had seen them. So he seated him upon the throne and entrusted his affairs to him.

It was also said that Qitfir died in those nights, so he (Yusuf) was appointed to his post, and he married Ra'il (Zulaykha), and he found her a virgin, and there were born to him from her Ifra'im and Misha.

(p-168) ﴿Said, "Appoint me over the treasuries of the land"﴾: give me charge of it; and the land is the land of Egypt. ﴿Indeed, I am a knowing guardian﴾ of it against those who do not deserve it; ﴿knowing﴾ of the ways of managing it. Perhaps he (peace be upon him), when he saw that he would inevitably be employed by him in his affairs, preferred the post whose benefits are widespread and whose returns are great. And in this is evidence for the permissibility of seeking a position and showing that one is ready for it, and of assuming it from the hand of a disbeliever when it is known that there is no way to establish the truth and govern the people except by relying on him. And it is related from Mujahid that the king embraced Islam at his hand.

﴿And thus We established Joseph in the land﴾, in the land of Egypt, ﴿to settle therein wherever he willed﴾: he would dwell in its regions wherever he desired. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 58:

﴿And the brothers of Joseph came﴾ It is related that when the king appointed him as his vizier (wazir), he established justice and strove to increase cultivation and to safeguard the grain stores, until the years of drought arrived and famine spread over Egypt, al-Sham and their surrounding regions. The people turned to him, and he first sold them grain in exchange for dirhams and dinars, until none of these remained with them; then in exchange for jewelry and precious stones; then in exchange for livestock; then in exchange for estates and properties; then in exchange for their persons, until he had enslaved them all. Then he presented the matter to the king, who said: "The decision is yours." So he set them free and returned their property to them. Canaan had been struck by what had struck the rest of the lands, so Ya'qub sent his sons, except Binyamin, to him to obtain provisions (al-mira).

﴿So they entered upon him, and he recognized them, but they were unaware of him﴾ That is, Yusuf recognized them, but they did not recognize him, due to the long time that had passed, their separation from him when he was young, their forgetting him, their assumption that he had perished, and the change in his condition from the state in which they had seen him when they parted from him, together with their little reflection on his features because of awe and grandeur.

﴿And when he had furnished them with their provisions﴾ he equipped them with their supplies and loaded their camels with what they had come for. The *jihaz* (provisions) is what is prepared of goods for travel, such as the equipment for a journey, what is carried from one town to another, and what a woman is adorned with when she is sent to her husband. It was also read as «بِجِهازِهِمْ» with a kasra.

﴿He said: "Bring me a brother of yours from your father."﴾ It is narrated that when they entered upon him, he said: "Who are you and what is your affair? Perhaps you are spies?" They said: "God forbid! We are only sons of one father, and he is an aged old man, a truthful (*siddiq*) prophet of the prophets, named Ya'qub." He said: "How many are you?" They said: "We were twelve, and one of us went out into the wilderness and perished." He said: "How many are you here?" They said: "Ten." He said: "Then where is the eleventh?" They said: "He is with our father, who consoles himself with him for the one who perished." He said: "Who will bear witness for you?" They said: "No one here knows us, so no one can testify for us." Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 62:

﴿And he said to his servants﴾ to his boys who measure out (the grain). Fityan (young men, servants) is the plural of fata (young man). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read ﴿lifityanihi﴾ (to his servants) as the plural of abundance (jam' al-kathrah), so that it accords with his words: ﴿Put their merchandise into their saddlebags﴾. For he appointed one (man) for each saddlebag to fill it with their merchandise with which they had bought the food; and it consisted of sandals and hides. He did this out of generosity and favour towards them, and to spare them from taking the price of the food from them, and out of fear that his father would not have anything with which they could return. ﴿So that they may recognise it﴾ so that they may recognise the obligation to return it (haqq radd). Or so that they may recognise it. ﴿When they return﴾ when they go back and return. ﴿To their families﴾ and open their sacks. ﴿So that perhaps they will come back﴾ so that perhaps their recognition of that will prompt them to return.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 63–64:

﴿When they returned to their father, they said: "O our father, the measure has been withheld from us, so send with us our brother that we may receive the measure."﴾ It was decreed that the measure be withheld from them after this, if we do not take Benjamin along. ﴿So send with us our brother, and we shall receive the measure﴾: we shall lift the barrier to receiving the measure, and receive what we need. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read yakhtal (with the ya'), as attributing it to the brother, meaning he will receive the measure for himself, so that his measuring is added to our measuring. ﴿And indeed we will be its guardians﴾: from anything disagreeable befalling him.

﴿He said: "Shall I entrust him to you except as I entrusted his brother to you before?" And you said about Joseph: "And indeed we will be its guardians."﴾

﴿"But Allah is the best guardian"﴾: so I rely upon Him and entrust my affair to Him. The accusative of "ḥifẓan" is as a specification (tamyiz), and "ḥāfiẓan" according to the reading of Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs may be taken as such, or as a circumstantial accusative (hal), like the saying: "How excellent is he as a horseman (lillahi darruhu fāriṣan)." It was also read "khayru ḥāfiẓin" and "khayru al-ḥāfiẓīn."

﴿"And He is the most merciful of the merciful"﴾: so I hope that He will show mercy to me by guarding him, and will not join two calamities upon me.
