Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 65:

﴿And when they opened their goods, they found their merchandise (bidaa'atahum) returned to them.﴾ It was also read "ridat" (with the kasrah of the assimilated dal transferred to the ra', as in "bi'a" and "qil"). ﴿They said: O our father, what more do we want?﴾ That is, what (ma dhā) do we seek? Is there any increase beyond this? He has honored us, treated our lodging well, sold to us, and returned our merchandise to us. Or: we do not seek beyond that any kindness, or: we do not exaggerate in speech and do not add to what we have related to you of his kindness.

It was also read "ma tabghi" in the second person, meaning: what (ayy shay') do you seek beyond this of kindness, or of proof of our truthfulness? ﴿This our merchandise has been returned to us﴾ is a resumptive clause explaining His words ﴿what more do we want?﴾ ﴿And we will bring provision for our family﴾ is coordinated with an omitted element, meaning: it has been returned to us, so we will strengthen ourselves with it and bring provision for our family by returning to the king. ﴿And we will guard our brother﴾ from dangers in our going and coming. ﴿And we will gain an extra camel-load﴾ (wasq ba'ir) by taking our brother along. This is if "ma" is interrogative; but if it is negative, that possibility remains, and it is also possible that the clauses are coordinated with "ma nabghi," meaning: we do not exaggerate in what we say, ﴿and we bring provision for our family, and guard our brother﴾.

﴿That is a small measure﴾, meaning: a small, insignificant measure that will not suffice us. They considered the measure given to them to be small, so they wished to double it by returning to the king and to have added for them what is measured for their brother. It is also possible that the reference is to the camel-load, meaning: that is a small thing that will not burden us with the king, nor will he regard it as great. It has also been said that this is from the words of Ya'qub, and its meaning is: the load of a camel is a small thing, not worth risking a son for.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 66:

﴿He said: "I will never send him with you"﴾ since I have seen from you what I have seen. ﴿Until you give me a solemn covenant (mawthiq) from God﴾ until you give me that by which I may bind myself, from God, that is, a covenant confirmed by mention of God. ﴿That you will surely bring him back to me﴾ this is the answer to the oath, since the meaning is: until you swear by God that you will surely bring him back to me. ﴿Unless you are surrounded﴾ unless you are overpowered and unable to do that, or unless you are all destroyed. This is an exceptive construction (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of circumstances, and the meaning is: "You shall surely bring him back to me in every circumstance, except the circumstance of being surrounded by you [i.e., of being destroyed]." Or it is from the most general of causes, with the sentence "You shall surely bring him back to me" understood as a negation, that is: "You will not refrain from bringing him, except because you are surrounded," like the saying of them: "I swear by God, unless you do it," meaning: "I seek nothing but your doing it."

﴿When they gave him their covenant﴾ their pledge. ﴿He said: "God is Witness to what we say"﴾ regarding the request for the covenant and the giving of it. ﴿Guardian (wakil)﴾ watchful, observing.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 67–68:

﴿And he said: "O my sons, do not enter through one gate, but enter through separate gates."﴾ Because they were people of beauty and stateliness, well known in Egypt for their nearness to and honor with the king, he feared that if they entered as one group they would be harmed (yu'anu, "be afflicted by the evil eye"). Perhaps he did not instruct them in this on the first occasion because they were unknown at that time; or the motive for it was his fear for Benjamin. Among the effects of the soul (al-nafs) is the evil eye (al-'ayn), and what indicates this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in his supplication: "O God, I seek refuge in the perfect words of God from every devil and noxious creature, and from every envious eye that harms."

﴿And I cannot avail you anything against God. Judgment belongs only to God.﴾ That is, against what He has decreed for you, even though I have pointed you to this course, for caution does not prevent destiny. ﴿Upon Him I have relied, and upon Him let those who rely put their trust.﴾ He combined the two particles (wa and fa) in conjoining one sentence to another, because the relative clause was placed first for specification (li'l-ikhtisas). It is as if the wa is for conjunction and the fa for indicating causation, since the act of the prophets is a cause for them to be followed.

﴿And when they entered from where their father had commanded them﴾ — that is, through separate gates in the city. ﴿It did not avail them﴾ — the opinion of Ya'qub and their following of it. ﴿Anything against God﴾ — against what He had decreed for them, as Ya'qub (peace be upon him) had said. Then they were robbed, and Benjamin was seized upon the finding of the drinking-bowl in his baggage, and the calamity upon Ya'qub was doubled. ﴿Except a need in the soul of Ya'qub﴾ — an exceptive clause of discontinuity (istithna' munqati'), meaning: but rather a need in himself, namely his compassion for them and his guarding them from being harmed. ﴿Which he fulfilled﴾ — he manifested it and enjoined it. ﴿And indeed he was a possessor of knowledge, because of what We had taught him﴾ — through revelation and the establishing of proofs. For this reason he said, ﴿And I cannot avail you anything against God,﴾ and he was not deceived by his own planning.

﴿But most people do not know﴾ — the secret of destiny, and that caution does not avail against it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 69:

﴿And when they entered upon Yusuf, he drew his brother to himself.﴾ He drew Binyamin to himself at the meal, or in the house. It is narrated that he hosted them and seated them two by two, so Binyamin was left alone. He wept and said: "If my brother Yusuf were alive, he would sit with me." So he seated him with himself at his table. Then he said: "Let each two of you go down to a house, and this one has no second, so he will be with me." So he spent the night with him, and said to him: "Would you like me to be your brother in place of your brother who perished?" He said: "Who would find a brother like you? But Ya'qub and Rahil did not give birth to you." Then Yusuf wept, rose to him, and embraced him, and ﴿said: "Indeed I am your brother, so do not be distressed."﴾ "Tabta'is" is an ifti'al (reflexive form) from al-bu's (distress), meaning do not grieve. ﴿for what they used to do﴾ against us in the past.

﴿So when he had furnished them with their provisions, he put the drinking-cup﴾, that is, the drinking bowl, ﴿into his brother's saddlebag﴾. It is said that it was a drinking bowl that was used as a measure (ṣā‘) with which grain is measured. It is also said that it was used to give water to the animals and for measuring, and that it was made of silver. It is also said that it was of gold. It is read as "wa-judhila" (passive, "and it was placed"), and the answer to "lammā" (when) is omitted; its implied meaning is: he gave them respite until they set off.

﴿Then a caller called out﴾, that is, a herald proclaimed: ﴿"O caravan, you are surely thieves!"﴾ Perhaps he did not say this on the command of Yusuf, peace be upon him, or the placing of the cup and the calling out about it took place with the consent of Binyamin. It is also said that the meaning is: "You are surely thieves of Yusuf from his father," or it is an interrogative: "Are you surely thieves?" The word ʿīr (caravan) means the company of travellers, and it is the name of the camels that carry loads, because they go back and forth (taʿīr, i.e., they travel to and fro). So it was applied to their owners, as in his saying, peace be upon him: "O horsemen of God, mount!"

It is also said that ʿīr is the plural of ʿīr (a donkey caravan), whose original form was faʿal, like saqaf, and it was treated as that form was treated in bayad. It was used figuratively for a caravan of donkeys, and then it was extended to any caravan.

﴿They said, turning towards them: "What is it that you are missing?"﴾ That is, what thing has been lost from you? Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 74–75:

﴿They said: "What is the penalty for it"﴾ "What is the penalty for the thief" (fa-ma jaza'u al-sariqi), or "for the theft" (aw al-sarq), or "for the cup" (aw al-sawa'), with the noun elided (ala hadhf al-mudaf). ﴿If you are liars﴾ in claiming innocence.

﴿They said: "Its penalty is: he in whose saddlebag it is found, he himself is its penalty"﴾ That is, the penalty for his theft is that the one in whose saddlebag it is found be seized and enslaved (ukhidha man wujida fi rahlihi wa-istirqaquhu). Thus was the law (shar') of Ya'qub, peace be upon him. His saying ﴿he himself is its penalty﴾ is an affirmation of the ruling and a binding of it upon him. Or it is the predicate (khabar) of ﴿man﴾, with the fa' (fa) being there because it implies the meaning of a conditional (li-tadammuniha ma'na al-shart), or it is the response (jawab) to it on the basis that it is conditional. The sentence, as it is, is the predicate of ﴿its penalty﴾, by placing the noun in the place of the pronoun (ala iqamat al-zahir fiha maqam al-damir), as if it had been said: "Its penalty is: he in whose saddlebag it is found, he is he." ﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾ for theft.

﴿So he began with their sacks.﴾ "He began" refers to the caller (al-mu'adhdhin). It was also said that it refers to Yusuf, because they had been sent back to Egypt. ﴿Before the sack of his brother﴾, Benjamin, to clear him of the accusation. ﴿Then he brought it out﴾, that is, the drinking-vessel (al-siqaya) or the measuring-bowl (al-suwa'), because the word is both masculine and feminine. ﴿From the sack of his brother.﴾ It is also read with a damma on the waw, and with the waw changed into a hamza (a glottal stop). ﴿Thus﴾, like that scheme. ﴿We devised for Yusuf﴾, by teaching him it and inspiring him with it. ﴿He could not take his brother under the king's law﴾, the king of Egypt's law, because his law was beating and fining double the value of what was taken, not enslavement. This clause explains the scheme.

﴿Except that God wills﴾, that He makes that ruling the king's ruling. The exception is from the most general of circumstances. It may also be a disjunctive exception (al-istithna' al-munqati'), meaning: but his taking him was by the will of God, the Exalted, and His permission. ﴿We raise in degrees whom We will﴾, by knowledge, just as We raised his rank. ﴿And over every possessor of knowledge is one who is All-Knowing﴾, one of higher rank than him. Whoever claims that God knows by His essence has used this as evidence, since if He were a possessor of knowledge, there would be someone above Him who knows more. The answer is that what is meant is every possessor of knowledge among creation, because the discussion concerns them, and because al-'Alim (the All-Knowing) is God, glory be to Him, whose meaning is the one to whom perfect knowledge belongs in the lexical sense. There is also no difference between this and our saying "above every scholar is one who is All-Knowing," and this is a specific (makhsus) statement.

They said, "If he steals," [Benjamin], "then a brother of his stole before," meaning Yusuf. It is said: his paternal aunt had inherited from her father the belt (mintaqah) of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. She used to nurse Yusuf and love him. When he grew up, Ya'qub wanted to take him from her, so she tied the belt around his waist, then pretended that it had been lost. It was searched for and found tied on him, so by their law she became more entitled to him. It is said that her maternal grandfather had an idol, which Yusuf stole, broke, and threw among the carrion. It is said that there was in the house a female goat or a hen, and he gave it to the beggar. It is said that he entered a church and took a small golden statue.

"So Yusuf kept it hidden within himself and did not reveal it to them." He concealed it and did not show it to them. The pronoun (dhamir) refers to the answer, or the statement, or the attribution of theft to him. It is said that it is a kinaya (allusion) whose explanation is given by the following clause, namely His saying, "He said, 'You are worse in position,'" for this is a substitute (badal) for "kept it hidden." The meaning is: he said within himself, "You are worse in position," that is, in rank regarding theft, because of your stealing your brother, or in evil conduct regarding what you were engaged in. Its feminine form is by consideration of the word or the sentence. There is in this a point for consideration, since what is explained by a sentence can only be a pronoun referring to the matter (dhamir al-sha'n).

"And God knows best what you describe." He knows that the matter is not as you describe.

"They said, 'O Chief of Egypt, indeed he has an aged father, so take one of us in his place. Indeed, we see you to be among the doers of good.'" That is, in years or in rank. They mentioned his circumstances to him, seeking his compassion for them.

"Take one of us in his place," in exchange for him, for his father is grief-stricken over his lost brother and finds comfort in this one. "Indeed, we see you to be among the doers of good" toward us, so complete your kindness; or, "among those accustomed to doing good," so do not change your habit.

He said, "[I seek] refuge in God that we take anyone but him with whom we found our property." For taking another would be an injustice according to your ruling. Had we taken one of you in his place, "indeed we would be wrongdoers" according to this view of yours. His meaning is that God permitted the seizing of the one in whose baggage we found the drinking cup, for his benefit and God's approval of him, so if I took someone other than him, I would be a wrongdoer.

(p-173) ﴿So when they despaired of him﴾, they had lost hope of Joseph and of his responding to them. The addition of the sīn and tā' (in istayʾasū) is for emphasis (mubālagha, intensification). ﴿They withdrew﴾: they went apart and isolated themselves. ﴿Conferring privately (najiyyan)﴾: conferring in private consultation. He used the singular form because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), or because it follows its pattern (bi-zinatihi), as it is said, "he is ṣiddīq." Its plural is anjiya, like nadiyy and andiya. ﴿Said the eldest of them﴾ in age, and he was Rūbīl; or in opinion, and he was Shamʿūn; and it is said he was Yahūdhā. ﴿Did you not know that your father had taken from you a solemn covenant (mawthiqan) in God's name﴾: a firm pledge. The reason their oath by God is called a mawthiq from Him is that it was with His permission and confirmation on His part.

﴿And before this﴾: and before this (present matter). ﴿You neglected [your duty] regarding Joseph﴾: you fell short in regard to his affair. The mā is superfluous (zā'ida), though it may be a verbal (maṣdariyya) particle in the accusative position by coordination with the object of taʿlamū (you knew). There is no harm in separating the coordinating particle from the coordinated element by an adverbial phrase. Alternatively, it may be in the position of the subject of inna, with its predicate in "Joseph," or in "from before" (min qablu). Or it is in the nominative by inception, with the predicate being "from before." But this is open to question, because qabl, when it is a predicate or a relative clause, is not cut off from the annexation (iḍāfa) so that it is not diminished. It may also be a relative pronoun (mawṣūla), meaning: what you did to him, that is, what you previously committed against him of wrongdoing, and its location is what precedes it. ﴿So I will not leave the land﴾: so I will not depart from the land of Egypt. ﴿Until my father gives me leave﴾ to return. ﴿Or God decides for me﴾: or He judges in my favour concerning departing from it, or concerning my brother's release from them, or concerning fighting alongside them to free him.

It is narrated that they spoke to the Governor about releasing him, and Rūbīl said: "O King, by God, you will either let us go, or I will cry out a cry by which pregnant women will miscarry." The hairs of his body stood up and came out of his garments. Then Joseph, peace be upon him, said to his son: "Get up beside him and touch him." Whenever one of the sons of Jacob, peace be upon him, became angry and another touched him, his anger would leave him. Then Rūbīl said: "Who is this? Surely in this land there is a seed from the seed of Jacob."

﴿And He is the best of judges﴾, because His judgment is never anything but in truth.

Al-Baydawi, *Anwar al-Tanzil*, on Surah 12, verses 81–82:

﴿Return to your father and say: "O our father, your son has stolen."﴾ According to what we witnessed of the outward appearance of the matter. It was recited as *Surriqa* (ṣurriqa, "he was accused of theft"), meaning he was attributed with theft (*al-sariqa*, "theft"). ﴿And we did not testify﴾ against him ﴿except to what we know﴾, namely that we saw the drinking cup (*al-ṣuwāʿ*) taken out of his bag. ﴿And we were not guardians of the unseen﴾, that is, of the inner reality of the situation. ﴿So we did not know that he stole or was falsely accused and the cup was planted in his baggage.﴾ Or, ﴿we were not knowers of the outcomes﴾, so when we gave you the covenant (*al-mawthiq*) we did not know that he would steal, or that you would be afflicted by him as you were afflicted by Joseph.

﴿Ask the town in which we were﴾, meaning Egypt, or a town near it where the crier caught up with them. The meaning is: send to its people and ask them about the story. ﴿And the caravan in which we came﴾, and the companions of the caravan with whom we set out and were with them. ﴿And indeed we are truthful﴾, an emphatic assertion in the place of an oath.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verses 83–84:

﴿He said: "Nay, but your own souls have made a matter seem good to you."﴾ That is, when they returned to their father and told him what their brother had said to them, he said: ﴿Nay, but your own souls have made it seem good to you.﴾ That is, they embellished it and made it easy. ﴿A matter (amran) that you yourselves had intended and planned.﴾ Otherwise, I do not know that the king would take the thief for his theft. ﴿So patience is most fitting (sabrun jamil).﴾ That is, my affair is patience that is fitting, or: patience that is fitting is more fitting. ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me﴾: Joseph, Benjamin, and their brother who remained in Egypt. ﴿Indeed He is the All-Knowing﴾ of my condition and theirs, ﴿the All-Wise﴾ in His management of both of them.

﴿And he turned away from them﴾ and withdrew from them, out of dislike for what he had encountered from them. ﴿And he said: "Oh, my grief over Joseph!"﴾ That is, "O my grief! Come, for this is your time." Al-asaf (grief) is the most intense sorrow and regret, and the alif is a substitute for the ya' of the first person. He grieved over Joseph specifically, rather than over his two brothers, even though the calamity that had befallen them was the same, because his loss was the foundation of all calamities and was fresh, taking hold of the very center of his heart, and because he was confident in their survival rather than his own. There is a hadith: "No nation among the nations has been given, at the time of calamity, [the words] 'Indeed we belong to Allah and to Him we return' except the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ)."

Do you not see that Ya'qub (peace be upon him), when what befell him befell him, did not say the words of return but said, ﴿Oh, my grief!﴾

﴿And his eyes turned white from the grief﴾: from the abundance of his weeping out of sorrow, as if the tears had erased their blackness. It is said that his sight became weak; it is also said that he became blind. It is also read as "min al-hazan" (from the grief). In this there is evidence for the permissibility of expressing sorrow and weeping at the time of shock. Perhaps such things do not fall under obligation, for few can control themselves in times of hardship. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wept over his son Ibrahim and said: "The heart grieves and the eye weeps, and we do not say what displeases the Lord; and indeed, O Ibrahim, we are saddened by you."

﴿So he was suppressing (kazim)﴾: filled with anger over his sons, holding it inside his heart without showing it. It is an intensive form (fa'il) in the sense of the passive (maf'ul), as in the verse ﴿and he is suppressed (maktum)﴾, from kazama the water-skin when he tied it tight over its contents; or in the sense of the active (fa'il), as in the verse ﴿and those who restrain their anger (al-kazimin al-ghaydh)﴾, from kazama al-ghayz when he swallowed it; and its root is kazama al-ba'ir jarrathu, when the camel returns its cud into its stomach.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 85:

﴿They said, "By Allah, you will not cease remembering Joseph"﴾ That is, "You will not cease, and you will never stop, remembering him in grief over him." The negative particle (لا, lā) has been omitted, as in the line of poetry:

"So I said, 'By the oath of Allah, I will not cease sitting.'"

This is because it would not be confused with the affirmative, for when an oath does not have the signs of the affirmative with it, it is understood as negative. ﴿Until you become ḥaraḍan﴾, meaning ill, close to ruin. It has also been said that ḥaraḍ is one whom grief or illness has melted away. It is originally a verbal noun (maṣdar), and for this reason it is not made feminine or pluralized. As a descriptive adjective it takes the vowel kasra, like danaf and danif (both meaning gravely ill). It has also been read with that vowel and with two ḍammas, like junub. ﴿Or you become among the ones who perish﴾, meaning among the dead.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verses 86–87:

﴿He said, "I only complain of my anguish (bathth) and my grief (huzn)"﴾: my distress (hamm), which I cannot bear patiently. Al-bathth here means spreading out (al-nashr). ﴿to Allah﴾: not to any of you or anyone else. So leave me and my complaint. ﴿And I know from Allah﴾: from His providence (sun'ihi) and mercy (rahmatihi), for He does not disappoint one who calls upon Him, nor does He abandon one who seeks refuge in Him. Or it means "from Allah" through a kind of inspiration (al-ilham). ﴿what you do not know﴾: about the life of Yusuf. It is said that he saw the Angel of Death in a dream, asked him about Yusuf, and he replied that he was alive. It is also said that he knew from Yusuf's dream that he would not die until his brothers prostrated to him.

﴿"O my sons, go and search for news (fatahassasu) of Yusuf and his brother"﴾: seek information about them and investigate their condition. Al-tahassus means seeking perception (talab al-ihsas). ﴿"And do not despair of the mercy (rawh) of Allah"﴾: do not lose hope in His relief (faraj) and ease (tanfis). It was also read as "min ruhi Allah" (from the spirit of Allah), meaning from His mercy by which He gives life to His servants. ﴿Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people﴾: those who deny Allah and His attributes. The knower of Allah who is a believer does not despair of His mercy in any circumstance.

(p-175)

﴿فَلَمّا دَخَلُوا عَلَيْهِ قالُوا يا أيُّها العَزِيزُ﴾ ["So when they entered upon him, they said: O Chief"], after they had returned to Egypt a second time. ﴿مَسَّنا وأهْلَنا الضُّرُّ﴾ ["Adversity has touched us and our family"], meaning the severity of hunger. ﴿وَجِئْنا بِبِضاعَةٍ مُزْجاةٍ﴾ ["And we have come with meager merchandise"], meaning inferior or scanty goods, which are rejected and pushed away out of disinterest in them. It derives from "azjaytuhu" (I pushed him), when I pushed him away, and from it comes "tazjiyat al-zaman" (the passing of time).

It was said that it was counterfeit dirhams (zuyuf, debased coins). It was said that it was wool and clarified butter. It was said that it was pine nuts and green seeds. It was said that it was dried curd and parched barley-meal (sawiq al-maql).

﴿فَأوْفِ لَنا الكَيْلَ﴾ ["So give us full measure"], meaning complete the measure for us. ﴿وَتَصَدَّقْ عَلَيْنا﴾ ["and be charitable to us"], either by returning our brother, or by overlooking the shortfall and accepting the inferior goods, or by giving more than the worth of what we brought. It has been disputed whether the prohibition on taking charity (ṣadaqah) applies to all the prophets, peace be upon them, or is specific to our Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ يَجْزِي المُتَصَدِّقِينَ﴾ ["Indeed, Allah rewards those who give charity"] with the best reward. Tasaddaq means to show bounty in general, and from this is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying concerning the palace: "This is a charity which Allah has given you, so accept His charity."

However, by custom it has become restricted to that which is given seeking a reward from Allah the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 89:

﴿He said: "Do you know what you did with Joseph and his brother?"﴾ That is: Did you know how ugly it was, so that you would repent of it? Their action toward his brother was to separate him from Joseph and to humiliate him, so that he could not speak to them except in helplessness and abasement. ﴿When you were ignorant﴾ of its ugliness, which is why you undertook it, or [it may mean] you punished him. He said this only as counsel to them and an incitement to repentance, out of compassion for them, seeing their helplessness and humble state, not as reproach and rebuke. It has also been said that they gave him the letter of Jacob concerning the release of Benjamin, and mentioned to him what he was suffering of grief over the loss of Joseph and his brother, and then he said this to them. He made them appear ignorant only because their action was the action of ignorant people, or because at that time they were young and reckless.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verses 90–91:

﴿They said: "Are you indeed Joseph?"﴾ This is a question of confirmation (istifham taqrir), and for this reason it is emphasized with inna and the lam being attached to it. Ibn Kathir read it as an affirmative statement. It is said they recognized him by his teeth and his features when he spoke to them. It is said he smiled and they recognized him by his front teeth (thana—the front teeth). It is also said he lifted the crown from his head, and they saw a mark on his forehead resembling a white beauty spot (shamah), and this was (a feature) of Sarah and Jacob, who had the like of it.

﴿He said: "I am Joseph, and this is my brother"﴾ mentioning him as a way of identifying himself through him, and of magnifying his status, and of including him in his words: ﴿Allah has indeed been gracious to us﴾, that is, with safety and honor. ﴿Indeed, he who is mindful of Allah﴾, that is, mindful of Allah, ﴿and is patient﴾, in trials or in acts of obedience and in abstaining from sins, ﴿then indeed Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers.﴾ He placed "the good-doers" (al-muhsinin) in the position of the pronoun, to alert to the fact that the good-doer is one who combines mindfulness (taqwa) and patience (sabr).

﴿They said: "By Allah, indeed Allah has preferred you over us"﴾, that is, He chose you over us with beauty of form and perfection of conduct. ﴿And indeed we were sinners﴾, and the situation is that our condition was: we were indeed guilty for what we did to you.

He said, "No reproach shall be upon you today." ﴿لا تَثْرِيبَ عَلَيْكُمُ﴾: *la ta'nib 'alaykum*, meaning no reproach (*ta'nib*) upon you. *Tathrib* is an intensive form (*taf'il*) derived from *al-tharb*, which is the fat that covers the stomach (*al-kirsh*). It is used for removal, like *tajlid* (flogging). It is therefore used metaphorically for the rebuke that tears at a person's honor and removes the water of the face. ﴿Today﴾ (*al-yawm*) is related either to ﴿tathrib﴾ or to the implied element of the prepositional phrase that serves as the predicate of ﴿no reproach﴾. The meaning is: I shall not reproach you today, which is the time when such reproach is expected, so what do you suppose about the other days? Alternatively, it is related to his words ﴿God will forgive you﴾, because he pardoned their offense at that time, and they had acknowledged it. ﴿And He is the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾: He forgives minor and major sins and bestows favor upon the penitent.

From the generosity of Joseph (peace be upon him): when they recognized him, they sent to him saying, "You invite us to food morning and evening, and we are ashamed before you because of what we did to you." He said, "The people of Egypt used to look at me with the first look and say, 'Glory be to Him who raised to this station a slave who was sold for twenty dirhams.' But I have been honored by you and magnified in their eyes, since they came to know that you are my brothers and that I am of the descendants (*hafadah*) of Abraham (peace be upon him)."

(p-176) ﴿Go with this shirt of mine﴾: the shirt that he was wearing. It is also said: it is the inherited shirt that was in the amulet.

﴿Cast it upon my father's face; he will return seeing﴾: that is, he will return with sight, i.e., possessing vision. ﴿And bring me﴾: you and my father. ﴿Your families, all of them﴾: with your women, your offspring and your dependents.

He said, "No reproach shall be upon you today." ﴿لا تَثْرِيبَ عَلَيْكُمُ﴾: *la ta'nib 'alaykum*, meaning no reproach (*ta'nib*) upon you. *Tathrib* is an intensive form (*taf'il*) derived from *al-tharb*, which is the fat that covers the stomach (*al-kirsh*). It is used for removal, like *tajlid* (flogging). It is therefore used metaphorically for the rebuke that tears at a person's honor and removes the water of the face. ﴿Today﴾ (*al-yawm*) is related either to ﴿tathrib﴾ or to the implied element of the prepositional phrase that serves as the predicate of ﴿no reproach﴾. The meaning is: I shall not reproach you today, which is the time when such reproach is expected, so what do you suppose about the other days? Alternatively, it is related to his words ﴿God will forgive you﴾, because he pardoned their offense at that time, and they had acknowledged it. ﴿And He is the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾: He forgives minor and major sins and bestows favor upon the penitent.

From the generosity of Joseph (peace be upon him): when they recognized him, they sent to him saying, "You invite us to food morning and evening, and we are ashamed before you because of what we did to you." He said, "The people of Egypt used to look at me with the first look and say, 'Glory be to Him who raised to this station a slave who was sold for twenty dirhams.' But I have been honored by you and magnified in their eyes, since they came to know that you are my brothers and that I am of the descendants (*hafadah*) of Abraham (peace be upon him)."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verses 94–95:

﴿And when the caravan set out﴾ from Egypt and departed from its settlements. ﴿Their father said﴾ to those present with him. ﴿Indeed, I find the scent of Joseph﴾. Allah caused him to perceive the scent of what clung to his shirt of his fragrance when Yahudha (Judah) brought it to him from eighty farsakhs (parasangs) away. ﴿Were it not that you think me senile﴾, that you attribute me to al-fanad (senility), which is a loss of mind that comes from old age. For this reason one does not say ʿajūz mufannada (a senile old woman), because the loss of her mind is inherent. The answer to ﴿لَوْلا﴾ (lawla, "were it not") is omitted, its estimated meaning being: "you would have believed me," or "I would have said that he is near."

﴿They said﴾, that is, those present. ﴿By Allah, you are indeed in your old error﴾, meaning you are indeed in your going astray from what is right, qudum (long-standing), through excess in loving Joseph, frequent mention of him, and anticipation of meeting him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 96:

﴿Then when the bearer of good tidings came﴾: this was Yahuda (Judah). It is related that he said: "Just as I saddened him by bringing him the shirt stained with blood, I will gladden him by bringing him this."

﴿He cast it over his face﴾: the bearer of good tidings cast the shirt over the face of Ya'qub (Jacob), peace be upon him, or Ya'qub himself did so. ﴿And he regained his sight﴾: he returned to seeing, because of the strength that revived in him. ﴿He said: Did I not tell you that I know from God what you do not know﴾: about the life of Yusuf (Joseph), peace be upon him, and the coming of joy. It has also been said that ﴿I know﴾ is a new, independent statement (kalam mubtada', كَلامٌ مُبْتَدَأٌ), and that what was said is (Do not despair of the mercy of God), or ﴿Indeed I find the scent of Yusuf﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verses 97–98:

﴿They said: "O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins. Indeed, we were sinners."﴾ It is the right of one who acknowledges his sin that the one wronged pardon him and ask for him forgiveness.

﴿He said: "I will ask my Lord for forgiveness for you. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."﴾ He postponed it until the last part of the night (al-sahar), or until the night prayer (salat al-layl), or until the night of Friday (laylat al-jumu'ah), seeking out the time of acceptance of supplication (ijabah). Or [he postponed it] until they had sought the pardon of Yusuf, or until he knew that he had pardoned them, for the pardon of the wronged party is a condition for forgiveness. This is supported by what is related: that he faced the qiblah standing and supplicating, and Yusuf stood behind him, and they stood behind the two of them, humbled and submissive, until Jibril descended and said: "Indeed, Allah has answered your supplication concerning your son, and has bound their covenant after you to prophethood." And this, if authentic, is evidence of their prophethood, and that what proceeded from them occurred before they were made prophets (istinba'ihim).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 99:

﴿When they entered upon Yusuf﴾ It is narrated that he sent to him mounts and wealth so that he might equip himself with those who were with him. Yusuf and the king went out to meet him with the people of Egypt. His sons who entered Egypt with him were seventy-two men and women. When they set out with Musa, peace be upon him, they numbered six hundred thousand, five hundred and some seventy men, besides the offspring and the aged.

﴿He took his parents to himself﴾ He drew his father and his maternal aunt to himself and embraced them. He treated her as a mother, just as the paternal uncle is treated as a father in His saying: ﴿the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq﴾. Or it is because Ya'qub, peace be upon him, married her after his mother, and a stepmother (al-rabba) is called a mother. ﴿And he said: Enter Egypt, if God wills, in security﴾ from famine and all kinds of hardship. The will (mashi'a) is connected to the entering qualified by security. The first entering was at a place outside the city when they met him.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 100:**

﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell down before him in prostration.﴾ (It was) a greeting and an honouring of him, for prostration was among them of the kind of that (practice).

It is said that its meaning is: they fell down in prostration on account of him, prostrating to God in thanks. It is also said that the pronoun (al-ḍamīr) refers to God Most High, and the waw (al-wāw) refers to his parents and brothers, and the raising (al-rafʿ) is later than the falling (al-khurūr), even though it is mentioned first in wording, for the sake of emphasis on his glorifying them both.

﴿And he said: O my father, this is the interpretation of my vision from before﴾ which I saw in the days of my youth.

﴿My Lord has made it true﴾ (ḥaqqan), meaning truthful. ﴿And He has been kind to me when He brought me out of the prison﴾ and he did not mention the well (al-jubb), lest it be a reproach to them. ﴿And He brought you from the desert﴾ (min al-badw), from the desert land (al-bādiya), because they were owners of livestock and people of the desert. ﴿After Satan had caused discord between me and my brothers﴾ he corrupted (affairs) between us and stirred them up; it is from the goading (nazgh) of the rider to the animal when he prods it and urges it to run. ﴿Indeed my Lord is Subtle (laṭīf) in what He wills﴾ subtle in arranging it for Him, for there is no difficult matter but that His will takes effect in it and it becomes easy by it. ﴿Indeed He is the All-Knowing﴾ of the existence of the interests and the arrangements, ﴿the All-Wise﴾ who does everything at its time and in a manner that calls for wisdom.

It is narrated that Joseph took his father, peace be upon them both, around his treasuries, and when he brought him into the treasury of the papers, he said: O my father, how disobedient you were to me, that these papers and what you wrote to me (were kept) at eight stages (of travel)? He said: Gabriel (Jibrīl), peace be upon him, commanded me. He said: Did you not ask him? He said: You are more open with him than I am; ask him. So Gabriel said: God commanded me to do that, because of your saying: ﴿And I fear that the wolf will eat him﴾. He said: Then why did you not fear Me?

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 101:

﴿My Lord, You have indeed given me of the kingdom﴾ some of the kingdom, namely the kingdom of Egypt. ﴿And taught me of the interpretation of events﴾ the books, or the dreams. The "min" (from) here is also partitive (li-l-tab'idh, "for partialness"), because he was not given all interpretation. ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ their creator (mubdi'uhuma). Its being in the accusative is either because it is an adjective of the vocative, or because it is a vocative in its own right. ﴿You are my Guardian﴾ my helper and the one who manages my affairs. ﴿In this world and the Hereafter﴾ or: the One who takes charge of me with blessing in both of them. ﴿Let me die in submission﴾ take my soul. ﴿And join me with the righteous﴾ among my forefathers, or with the righteous in general in rank and honour.

It is narrated that Ya'qub, peace be upon him, remained with him twenty-four years. Then he died, and he had instructed that he be buried in al-Sham beside his father. So he (Yusuf) took him and buried him there, then returned and lived after him twenty-three years. Then his soul longed for the everlasting kingdom, so he wished for death, and Allah took his soul pure and clean. The people of Egypt then disputed about his burial place until they nearly came to fighting. They resolved to place him in a chest of marble and bury him in the Nile in a place where the water would flow over him, then it would reach Egypt, so that they would be a share in him. Then Musa, peace be upon him, transferred him to the burial place of his forefathers, and his age was one hundred and twenty years. He had begotten from Ra'il Ifra'im and Misha, and he is the grandfather of Yusha' ibn Nun, and Rahmah, the wife of Ayyub, peace be upon him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 12, verses 102–103:

﴿That﴾ refers to what has been mentioned of the account of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and the address in it is to the Messenger (ﷺ). It is the subject (*mubtada'*, the grammatical subject of the sentence). ﴿from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you﴾ are its two predicates (*khabaran*, the two grammatical predicates of the subject). ﴿And you were not with them when they resolved upon their affair while they were scheming﴾ serves as evidence for both of them. The meaning is: this account is unseen, and you did not know it except through revelation, because you were not present with the brothers of Yusuf when they resolved on what they planned, namely to put him in the bottom of the well, while they were scheming against him and against his father, so that he would send him with them. It is known, and not hidden from those who deny you, that you did not meet anyone who had heard that and then learned it from him. This second part was omitted because it is understood from its mention in other than this story, like His saying: ﴿You did not know it, neither you nor your people, before this﴾.

﴿And most of the people, even if you were eager﴾ for their faith and exerted yourself in displaying the signs to them, ﴿will not be believers﴾, because of their obstinacy and their determination to persist in disbelief.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verses 104–105:

﴿And you do not ask them for it﴾ — for the news (of the past) or for the Qur'an. ﴿any reward﴾ — any wage, as the transmitters of reports (akhbar) do. ﴿It is nothing but a reminder﴾ — an admonition from God, Exalted is He. ﴿to the worlds﴾ — to all of them, in general.

﴿And how many a sign﴾ — and how many a sign. The meaning is: however great a number of the indicators you wish, indicating the existence of the Creator (al-Sani'), His wisdom, the perfection of His power and His oneness. ﴿in the heavens and the earth they pass by﴾ — over them, passing over the signs and witnessing them. ﴿and they turn away from them﴾ — they do not reflect upon them, nor take heed from them.

It is read ﴿wal-ardi﴾ (and the earth) in the nominative, as a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is ﴿yamurruna﴾ (they pass by), so that the pronoun in ﴿alayha﴾ refers to it. It is also read in the accusative, meaning "and they tread upon the earth." And it is read "al-arda yamshuna alayha" (they walk upon the earth), meaning they move about in it and so see the traces of the destroyed nations.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verses 106–108:

﴿And most of them do not believe in God﴾ except in the sense of acknowledging His existence and that He is the Creator. ﴿Except that they associate others with Him﴾ by worshipping other than Him, or by taking the rabbis as lords. It is also said to refer to attributing a son (tabanni, adoption) to Him, the doctrine of light and darkness, looking only to secondary causes, and the like. It is said that the verse concerns the polytheists of Makkah, and it is said that it concerns the hypocrites, and it is said that it concerns the People of the Book.

﴿Do they then feel secure that there will not come upon them an overwhelming punishment from God﴾: a punishment that will cover them and encompass them. ﴿Or that the Hour will not come upon them suddenly﴾: unexpectedly, without any prior sign. ﴿While they are unaware﴾ of its coming, not prepared for it.

﴿Say: This is my way﴾, that is, calling to monotheism and preparing for the Return. For this reason he explained "the way" by His saying: ﴿I call to God﴾. It is also said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun (ya) of "I". ﴿With insight﴾: with clear evidence and a manifest proof, not blind. ﴿I﴾ is an emphasis for the hidden pronoun in ﴿I call﴾, or [it is an emphasis for the pronoun in] ﴿with insight﴾, since it is a circumstantial clause from it, or it is a subject whose predicate is ﴿with insight﴾. ﴿And whoever follows me﴾ is conjoined to it. ﴿And glory be to God; and I am not of the polytheists﴾: I exalt Him with complete exaltation above partners.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah (chapter) 12, verse 109:

﴿We did not send before you except men﴾: a refutation of their saying, ﴿If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels﴾. It was also said that its meaning is the negation of prophethood for women, that ﴿to whom We reveal, as We reveal to you﴾, and that they are distinguished thereby from others. Ḥafṣ recited ﴿nūḥī﴾ (We reveal) throughout the Qur'an, and Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī agreed with him in the surah of al-Anbiyā'. ﴿From the people of the towns﴾, because their people are more knowledgeable and more forbearing than the people of the desert. ﴿Have they not travelled in the land and seen how was the end of those before them﴾, of those who denied the messengers and the signs, so that they would beware of denying you; or, of those who were infatuated with the world and obsessed with it, so that they would desist from loving it. ﴿And the abode of the Hereafter﴾: "the abode of the Hereafter" means the abode of the state, or the Hour, or the afterlife. ﴿Is better for those who are mindful﴾ of shirk and sins. ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾: they use their intellects so that they recognize that it is better. Nāfi', Ibn 'Āmir, 'Āṣim and Ya'qūb read it with the letter tā' (taʿqilūn, "you reason"), by analogy with His saying: ﴿Say: This is my way﴾, i.e., say to them: "Will you not then reason?"

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 110:

﴿Until, when the Messengers despaired﴾ — the limit (ghayah) of a omitted element, indicated by the context; that is: let not the prolonged passage of their days deceive them, for those before them were also given respite until the Messengers despaired of victory over them in this world, or of their faith, because they were immersed in disbelief, living in luxury, persisting in it without any restraint. ﴿And they thought that they had been denied﴾ — that is, their own selves denied them when they told them that they would be victorious, or the people denied them the promise of faith. It was also said that the pronoun refers to those addressed by the messengers, meaning: those to whom the messengers were sent thought that the messengers had lied to them regarding the call and the warning. It was also said that the first refers to those to whom the messengers were sent and the second to the messengers, meaning: they thought that the messengers had lied and failed in what had been promised to them of victory, and the matter became confused for them. As for what is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that the messengers thought that they had been left unfulfilled in what Allah had promised them of victory: if it is authentic, then by "thought" he meant what passes through the heart by way of whispering (waswasah). Moreover, what is meant is an exaggeration of the delay and respite, by way of illustration. Other than the Kufans read it with the doubled letter (tashdid), meaning: the Messengers thought that the people had lied to them in what they had threatened them with. It was read "kadhabū" with the single letter (takhfif) and the active form of the verb, meaning: they thought that they had lied in what they had reported to their people when it was delayed from them and they saw no sign of it. ﴿There came to them Our help, and whom We willed was delivered﴾ — the Prophet and the believers; and He did not specify them, to indicate that they are the ones deserving that He should grant their deliverance, and no one else shares in it with them. Ibn ʿAmir, ʿAsim and Yaʿqub read it in the past tense with the passive form (mabni lil-maf'ul), and it was read "fa-naja" (and was delivered). ﴿And Our punishment is not turned back from the guilty people﴾ — when it descends upon them; and in it is an explanation of the two wills (mashiʼatayn).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 111:

﴿Indeed, in their stories﴾ — in the stories of the prophets and their peoples, or in the story of Yusuf and his brothers. ﴿there is a lesson for people of understanding﴾ — for those of sound intellect, freed from the impurities of habituation and of inclination toward the senses. ﴿It was not a narration that could be invented﴾ — the Qur'an was not a narration that could be invented. ﴿but a confirmation of what came before it﴾ — of the divine books. ﴿and a detailed explanation of all things﴾ — of what is needed in the religion, for there is no religious matter except that it has a basis in the Qur'an, either through an intermediary or without one. ﴿and a guidance﴾ — from error. ﴿and a mercy﴾ — by which the good of both abodes is attained. ﴿for a people who believe﴾ — who accept it as true.

And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Teach your slaves (arqqa'akum) the Surah of Yusuf, for whatever Muslim recites it and teaches it to his family and to those his right hand possesses, Allah will ease for him the agonies of death and will grant him the strength not to envy a Muslim."
